paragraphs.text: Again, with hope in God, we write the discourse on the soul, composed as best he could by the holy Mar Moses, the bishop surnamed Bar Kepha.

“Soul,” then, is a term with several meanings. It is used in many senses in Scripture and in accordance with nature and customary usage. “Soul” is used of God's nature, as when the Lord says through Isaiah the prophet, “My soul hates your festivals and your new moons,” and as in, “The Lord of lords has sworn by his soul.” This does not mean that God has a human soul. Far from it! Rather, here divine Scripture calls God's nature and being “soul.” The whole human being, composed of soul and body, is also called a “soul.” As it is written in Ezekiel the prophet, “The soul that sins shall die.” Here Scripture calls the whole composite being a “soul.” This is clear from the fact that death is the dissolution of the composite being. The body alone is also called a “soul,” when names and experiences are transferred from death to the dead, because of the union of the parts with one another. Thus it is written in David concerning Joseph, “His soul entered into iron.” Blood, too, is called “soul,” as when Moses says, “The soul of all flesh is blood.” Here he calls blood alone “soul.” The nourishing and growing power found in trees, grass, crops, and everything that receives nourishment and grows is also called “soul.” The philosophers call it “endowed with soul” and “animate.” This power is called the vegetative soul. Again, the name “soul” is given also to the power of sensation and movement found in all animals. This power is called the animal and elemental soul. It is called “animal” because the wise teachers of the Church call everything that senses, moves from place to place, and lives an animal, as do the philosophers outside the Church. It is called “elemental” because its composition comes from a combination of the elements. This animal and elemental soul belongs to all irrational animals and also to human bodies. The rational soul within us is also called “soul.” Through it we receive the law, and it distinguishes good from evil and truth from falsehood. It governs the body and enables it to move rationally. Thus “soul” is used in seven senses in divine Scripture and in writings and customary usage. These seven senses can be understood still more clearly from the classification set out below: 1. God's being and nature, as in: “My soul hates your festivals and your new moons.” 2. The whole human being, as in: “The soul that sins shall die.” 3. The body alone: “A satisfied soul tramples honeycombs.” 4. Blood alone: “The soul of all flesh is blood.” 5. The vegetative soul: (The nourishing and growing power found in trees and grass.) 6. The animal soul: the power of sensation and movement that [?] animals and bodies. 7. The rational soul: [?] we distinguish good from evil and move rationally. Our subject in this book, however, is the rational soul, not these other kinds. Showing that the soul exists. Someone may ask here, “How do we know that the soul exists, since it cannot be perceived by any of the senses?” For it cannot be seen with the eyes or heard with the ears. Nor can it be tasted with the palate, felt with the hand, or smelled with the nostrils. “Then,” someone says, “how is it known that the soul exists?” First, it is known that the soul exists from its name, namely “soul.” A name signifies something. And “soul” is a name. Therefore the name “soul” signifies something. But if someone objects and says that “it does not exist” is also a name, and therefore “it does not exist” signifies something, we say that “it does not exist” is not a name, but [?] “it exists” is a name. And “not” has been added to it; [?] “it does not exist” is not a name. But if he objects and says that there is a name [?] something, such as “goat-stag,” which is a name [?] signifying something, since [?] something composed of a goat and a stag, we say again that [?] “goat-stag” [?] does not signify a nature composed of a goat and a stag, since nothing of this kind exists. Rather, it signifies mere composite thoughts, compounded from a goat and a stag, as Aristotle said that names signify thoughts. It has therefore been shown that a name signifies something, and “soul” is [?]. Therefore the name “soul” signifies something. Thus it has become clear that the soul exists. It is also known that the soul exists from the fact that we see the body sometimes moving and sometimes ceasing its movement. While it is alive, it moves; but when it is dead, it ceases its movement. Now its movement comes either from itself or from another nature. If it came from itself, it would not at some point cease moving. It is clear that something else moves it, namely the soul. But if someone objects [?] that the body's movement comes from its elements, we say that it should then not cease moving until its elements are dissolved and separated from one another, and its parts are scattered, if these are the cause of its movement, as you claim. But if we see it cease moving while its elements have not yet been dissolved and scattered, it is clear that its movement comes from something else, namely the soul. Again, someone objects: “Look, we also see non-rational animals moving at one time and not moving at another. That is, while they are alive, they move; when they are dead, they cease moving. Then they too must have a rational soul that moves their bodies.” We say to him that these animals are not moved by a rational soul, as human bodies are, but by some other cause, as we will show with God's help, and as we showed in the first chapter: the soul of non-rational animals is a power of sensation and movement. This is the cause of their bodies' movement, and it is called the animal soul. But if he objects again and says that this animal soul also moves human bodies, we say that a rational soul moves human bodies, whereas an animal soul moves the bodies of non-rational animals. This is known from the fact that the rational soul enables human beings to move rationally, whereas the animal soul enables animals to move non-rationally. Rational movement differs from non-rational movement in many ways. For a human being is distinct in eating, drinking, and mating rationally. Everything that moves is moved either from within or from outside. What is moved from outside is like a millstone moved by mules or water. But what is moved from within— is like fire, which moves by its own nature and of itself. What is moved from outside stops moving from time to time, but what is moved from within does not stop. The body, then, is not moved from outside. This is clear from the fact that it is not simply pushed or dragged like things without a soul, which are pushed and dragged when something outside moves them. It remains, then, that it is moved from within. Although it is moved from within, it is not moved by its own nature, as fire moves by its own nature, but by something else. It is clear that fire moves by nature from the fact that it does not stop moving as long as it remains fire. The body, however, does not move by nature. This is clear from the fact that it stops moving while it remains a body. Therefore, if the body is neither moved from outside like things without a soul nor moved by nature like fire, it remains that it is moved by a soul, which is also the cause of its life. We are like stones and iron in being material bodies, but we differ from them in having sensation. We are like animals also in moving from place to place, in life, sight, hearing, and the other senses, and [?]; like them, we become angry and feel desire. In what, then, do we differ from them? Clearly, in having a rational soul. Therefore, the soul exists. Either the whole human being is mortal and subject to decay, or the whole is immortal and not subject to decay, or one part is mortal and subject to decay while another part is immortal and not subject to decay. Or we may call the soul the human being, as [?] Plato. The whole human being is mortal and subject to decay. Or we may call the body alone the human being, as the Stoics say. But part of the human being is mortal and subject to decay, as Pilate says, which is the truth. It is therefore clear that a soul exists from the fact [?] that of the human being is mortal and subject to decay— the body; but another part is immortal and not subject to decay—the soul. The wise acknowledge that substances and accidents exist. Some of these are perceived by the senses, while others are grasped by the mind, whether substances or accidents. For accidents must subsist in substances, because they have no existence of their own apart from substances. It is also acknowledged that blackness, whiteness, and the rest exist, as do goodness, evil, justice, and injustice. Whiteness and blackness, and corporeal things [?] (in a body), subsist simply. Health and sickness subsist in an animate body. But in what do goodness, evil, justice, and injustice subsist? Clearly, in the soul. If whiteness and blackness, which are accidents perceived by the senses, subsist in a material body, which is a substance perceived by the senses, then justice and injustice, which are accidents grasped by the mind, must also have a substance grasped by the mind in which to subsist. Therefore, the soul exists. It is also clear that a soul exists from its activity. How so? A person often closes the eyes of his body and sees inwardly with other eyes. His mouth is silent, yet he speaks in his heart, blessing whomever he wishes and cursing whomever he wishes. Again, while he is on earth, he sees the things in heaven [?] as he meditates. And while he is close at hand, he travels to distant places and sees what is there, without his body moving. Again, there are times when his tongue is silent, yet he brings the thoughts of his heart into the open and makes them known through writings. Again, we see a physician touching the sick person's visible body with his hand, and discovering the hidden suffering and pain. All these activities, and others like them, belong not to the body but to the soul. Again, the existence of the soul is evident from the invention of crafts. For where do metalworking, architecture, carpentry, and weaving come from, as well as geometry, astronomy, arithmetic, music, and all the other crafts, if not from the rational soul? But if someone objects and says that irrational animals also have crafts—for example, the bee in its construction of the honeycomb, the spider in its marvelous weaving, and the ant in its gathering of grain—we give him two answers. First, irrational animals do these things by nature, compelled by the force of nature, and not voluntarily through a rational soul. Human beings, however, learn crafts voluntarily through a rational soul, and not because they are compelled by the force of nature. Second, irrational animals have no need of teachers and pupils to practice their crafts, whereas human beings need masters and disciples. All these are inventions of the rational soul. Again, the existence of the soul is evident from its capacity to think ahead, and from its bringing this thought into action through the body, which is its instrument, and impressing it upon matter. For example: Often a carpenter first looks in his mind at the chair he wants to make, outlining its shape, height, depth, width, beauty, usefulness, and the rest. Afterward, through his own hands, an adze, wood, and movement, he puts into practice what he had previously fashioned according to his wish. It is the same with an architect when he wants to build a house, and with a smith when he wants to [?] an iron nail. This capacity to think ahead therefore belongs to the rational soul. Consequently, the soul exists. Again, the existence of the soul is evident from the two opposing activities found in a human being. For example, a person is often hungry but does not eat, thirsty but does not drink, and desires sexual intercourse but does not have intercourse. All these are activities of the body. What kind of desire is it when the body desires to eat and drink, yet does not eat or drink, unless there is another nature that restrains it from doing so? And what is the reason that the body desires to sleep or to have sexual intercourse, yet neither sleeps nor has intercourse, unless there is another nature that holds it back from doing so? This is not found in irrational animals. When a donkey is hungry and finds straw or barley, it cannot refrain from eating. And when it desires to mate and finds an opportunity to do so, it cannot refrain from mating, because it has no rational soul to restrain it from its irrational impulses. When someone is hungry and finds food but does not eat, or is thirsty and finds something to drink but does not drink, it is the body that desires. What restrains it from its desire is not the body. The body wants to eat, but what makes it abstain from its desire is not the body. The body wants to have sexual intercourse, but what keeps it chaste is not the body. For the body flees from blows and death, but what hands it over to death and blows in the hope of something is not the body. This is something [?] of that which is the soul. Again, likewise, because a human being has a rational soul, he can act or refrain from acting. For often, while his eyes are looking, he closes them so that they do not see; and while his ears are hearing, he stops them so that they do not hear. But irrational animals cannot control whether they see or do not see, or whether they hear or do not hear. Thus it has been demonstrated that there is a soul. If, then, a human being has two opposing activities, one supporting the body and the other opposing it, it is clear that this

activity, which opposes that of the body, belongs to the soul. But if someone objects and says that these two opposing activities come from the elements, we say to him that these elements, from which a human being is composed, do not oppose one another in the impulse of desire as the activity of the soul opposes the activity of the body. Sometimes, for example, the body wants to eat, but the soul does not allow it to eat, for whatever reason it chooses. We see that irrational animals fear human beings, work for them, and submit to them, even though they are equal to human beings in everything that comes from the elements. Yet no species of animal submits to and works for another and supplies its needs as it submits to a human being and supplies his needs. It is clear that this is because there is in him another nature, stronger than his elements, namely, the soul. This is why animals submit to him and serve him as slaves. It is also clear that there is a soul in a human being from the fact that he constructs syllogisms and distinguishes truth from falsehood and good from evil. It is clear that there is a soul from

the definition of a human being: a rational, mortal living being. He is called living and rational because of the soul, but mortal because of the body. Each of the organs through which the bodily senses operate has one activity: the eyes have seeing; the ears, hearing; the mouth, tasting; the nostrils, smelling; and the hands, touching. But which of the things the eyes see and the ears hear is beneficial, and which is not beneficial, and which of the things the hands touch is good and useful, and which is harmful— this (activity) of examining and distinguishing does not belong to the senses, nor to the body, but to the rational soul, which distinguishes what belongs to us from what does not, and what is beneficial from what is not beneficial. [?] There are six lines here that have been erased and cannot be read. [?] bodily [?] hot [?] and cold things from soft things [?], and salty things from tasteless things, and so on. But spiritual things are higher than it. I mean those that help and benefit, and those that do not, those that are good and useful, and those

that are not. The rational soul distinguishes them, not the body. But if someone again objects and says that this discernment is the constitution of the body, we say to him: Then this discernment ought to be found more in elephants and camels than in small animals. Yet we see that the small ones are more cunning, as in the case of the fox. It is clear that a human being has a soul from the fact that laws are laid down for him concerning what he should do and what he should not do, something that cannot happen with irrational animals. No one lays down a law for ravens (ravens) that they must not steal, or for doves that they must not commit sexual immorality. Or turtledoves to preserve chastity, or lambs to be gentle and humble, or donkeys to fast and pray. But a human being, because he has a rational soul, [?]. It is known that a human being has a soul from the fact that he fears hell [?] the kingdom. And he does good [?] when he sins [?]. These clearly belong to a rational soul, which distinguishes them and carries them out. These serve as natural and rational proofs. We also show from Holy Scripture that there is a soul. Moses said: “He formed—

the Lord God—Adam from the soil, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and Adam became a living soul.” David sang: “Bless the Lord, my soul”; and “His spirit departs, and he returns to his earth”; and “But you, my soul, will rejoice in God.” And “Praise the Lord, my soul.” Solomon said: “The body returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit to the Lord who gave it.” And again: “The souls of the righteous are in the hands of God.” Zechariah said: “He created the spirit of a human being within him.” Elijah said: “Lord God, let the boy’s soul return within him.” Hananiah and his companions said: “Souls and spirits of the righteous, bless the Lord.” Ezekiel said: “Come, spirit, from the four winds, and breathe upon the slain, so that they may live.” And the Lord said: “What will a person gain if he acquires the whole world but loses his soul?” And “They cannot kill the soul.” Stephen said: “They numbered seventy-five souls.” Peter said: “You have now returned to the shepherd of your souls.” John also said: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves.” Paul said: “Not a single soul among you will perish.” And again: “Let us cleanse ourselves from filth in holiness of spirit.”

Showing the views and thoughts

of the pagan teachers about the soul.

Now, among the pagan philosophers, some held and said that the soul is a body. Others said that it is incorporeal. Among those who said that it is a body, some said that it is a single element. Others said that it is composed of many elements. Among those who said that it consists of a single element, some said that it consists of water. This was Thales. Others said air; this was Anaximenes [?]. Others said that it is fire. This was Heraclitus. But none of them dared to say that the soul consists of earth, because of the great opposition between the subtlety of the soul and the nature of earth. As for those who said that it is composed of many elements, some said that it is the blood around the heart. This was Empedocles [?]. Others said that it is breath. This was Hippocrates [?]. Others said that it is a combination of tiny bodies flying through the air. This was Democritus. All these, then, who said that the soul is a body were Stoics, who said that everything is a body. They even said that God himself is a subtle body.

Those who said that the soul is incorporeal are also divided: some said that it is a substance, existing in and of itself, and that it does not need something else in order to exist. Others said that it is not a substance, since it does not exist in and of itself, but in something else. As for those who said that it is a substance existing in and of itself, And they said that it has a nature of its own, which moves and lives and has activity of itself and in its own right. As for those who said that it is not a substance in its own right but subsists in something else, some of them said that it is like sight in the eye and whiteness in snow, and like sweetness in [?]. Some of them said that it is the power of the mixture of the elements, [?] the activity produced by their combination, which was not present in each one of them separately and in its own right. For example, when honey, wine, and pepper are mixed together, an activity is produced from them which none of them possessed individually before. And just as, when many medicinal roots are mixed and blended, an effect is produced from them which was not present in any one of them before they were blended, so too, when the elements are mixed in equal proportions, a body is constituted from them, and from their mixture a power is produced which was not present in any one of them

before. This power is the nature of the soul. And just as, they say, activity, effect, or power perishes when separated from the things in which it subsists, so too the soul, when separated from the body, perishes. This, then, was the opinion of Alexander of Aphrodisias. Some of them said that the soul is the harmony of the combination of the elements. They derived this from the analogy of the harmony produced by the orderly striking of the strings of a lyre. And just as, they say, the lyre [?], when the strings of the lyre are separated from it, [?], so neither does the soul after it is separated from the body. This was the opinion of Acrates [?]. Some of them said that it is the entelechy of the body, that is, the completion of this form of the body. The one who held this view was Aristotle. It is therefore right [?] this. Aristotle said that there are three substances. One of them is the underlying matter. Another is the shape and form by which matter is moved. Another is that which is composed of these two, namely, matter and form. The substance which is matter he calls potentiality, because it is capable

of receiving shape. But the substance which is shape and form he calls entelechy, because it is the completion of the body. As an illuminating illustration of these statements of Aristotle, conceive of matter in your mind as solid, unformed bronze that has not yet received any shape at all. For form and shape, take the shape of a statue; for substance, take that which is composed of bronze and shape. Thus Aristotle understood it in three ways: (1) One is matter, which he called potentiality, like bronze that has not been shaped or worked in relief. (2) Another is form and shape, which he calls entelechy, like shape, configuration, and form. (3) Another is that which is composed of matter and form, like a statue composed of bronze and the shape of a human being. Aristotle therefore said that the soul is an entelechy in this sense, because it is the completion and form of the body. Just as, he says, the shape and form of a statue, and its shaping and completion as a statue,

come about when the bronze passes from what it was potentially into actuality, and therefore constitute the substance proper to the statue, so too the soul is the completion and form of the body. And therefore, he says, it is the entelechy of the body. And again, just as sight, when it comes into being, perfects the eye, so the soul, when it comes into being, perfects the living creature. These are among the opinions and thoughts that the pagan philosophers conceived and considered concerning the soul. These things become clearer from the classification outlined below: some said that the soul is a body. Some said that it is a single element, while others said that it is many elements. Some said that it is fire: Heraclitus. Others said that it is air: Anaximenes. Others said that it is made of water: Ampracletus [?]. Others said that it is a blowing wind: Acrates [?]. Others said that it is a combination of tiny bodies flying through the air: Democritus [?]. Some said that it is incorporeal. Of these, some said that it subsists independently, in its own existence. Others said that it is the harmony of the interweaving of the elements: Anacrates [?]. Others said that it is the actuality of the body: Aristotle. Others said that it is the power of the balanced mixture of the elements: Alexander of Aphrodisias. Some said that it does not subsist independently (some described it as being like sight in the eye), but subsists in something else.

There are others, however, who held other opinions that do not fall within this classification and are not included under it. Asclepiades said that the soul is the exercise of sensation. Pythagoras said that the soul is a number that moves itself. Others said that the soul is a collection of concepts and memories. Just as, they say, an unwritten sheet or scroll is capable of receiving writing and concepts, because these are written and imprinted on it, so too, when the human body is formed, it has neither thought nor understanding nor aptitude [?]. Later, however, the experiences it encounters gradually produce in it a collection of thoughts and concepts. This memory, they say, is the soul. Plato also said: There is a rational soul even in irrational animals. The Manichaeans also expressed these three opinions (thoughts) concerning the soul: first, that the soul is incorporeal; second, that it is immortal; and third, that the soul is one, they say, but is divided and comes to be in each individual body. Animate things share in it abundantly, while inanimate things share in it only a little. The heavenly bodies, however, share in it abundantly and to a great extent. Fourth Discourse

Against these opinions of the philosophers that have been stated. And a refutation of these firmly held opinions that they expressed concerning the soul. First, we address all those Stoics who say that the soul is a body. The Stoics, then, put forward three arguments by which they demonstrate that the soul is a body. Their first argument. They say that we resemble our fathers, not only in body but also in soul—that is, in emotion, habit, and disposition. Resemblance, however, belongs to bodies, not to what is incorporeal. Therefore, they say, the soul is a body. We refute their first argument as follows: similarity and dissimilarity are properties of quality. And quality is incorporeal, because what is incorporeal is similar or dissimilar to what is incorporeal. Second argument. They say that nothing incorporeal is affected together with a body when it becomes ill or is cut. But the body is affected together with the soul when it is affected. For example: When the soul is upset, the body reddens, and when it is afraid, the body sweats. Therefore, they say, the soul is a body, because it is affected together with the body. Refutation: First, against their first assertion, we say that there are incorporeal things that are affected together with bodies. For example, qualities,

which are incorporeal, are affected together with bodies. They too become qualities together with them [?], and when the bodies are heated, they are heated together with them. Next, against their second assertion, we say this: when the body is affected, it receives from the soul the sensation by which it feels, while the soul itself remains unaffected and does not suffer [?]. Third argument: Death, they say, is the separation of the soul from the body. Nothing incorporeal is separated from a body, nor is it attached to a body. But the soul is attached to the body and is also separated from it. Therefore, they say, the soul is a body. Refutation: What you said—that death is the separation of the soul from the body—is true. But what you then said—that something incorporeal is neither attached to a body nor separated from it—is false. For a line and whiteness, which are incorporeal, are attached to a body and separated from it. We also say that the soul is not attached to the body by mere contact. For if it were attached to it by contact, it would be positioned next to it or at its side. Again, if it were attached to it by contact, the whole body would not be endowed with soul, nor would the whole of it be alive. Rather,

only one part of it would be endowed with soul and alive: the part in contact with the soul. But if the whole body is endowed with soul and alive, the soul is united with all of it and bound to all of it, and is not attached to it by mere contact. These, then, are the three arguments of the Stoics and our refutation. Our demonstrations showing that the soul is not a body are these: 1. Every body, whatever it may be, falls under one of the senses or under all of them, and is therefore perceptible by the senses. But the soul is not perceptible by the senses: it is neither seen nor touched, and so on. Therefore it is not a body. 2. When one body is added to another body, it adds weight to it. But the soul is present in the body, and not only does it add no weight to it, but it actually gives it life and makes it light. Therefore it is not a body. 3. A body does not pass through another body, because each blocks the other, and their parts obstruct one another. But the soul passes through the whole body and dwells throughout it. Therefore it is not a body. 4. Every body that moves is moved either from outside, like a millstone that is pushed from outside, or from within, like a body endowed with soul. Now the soul is not moved from outside

like a body without soul. Therefore it is not a body. But if someone says that the soul is moved from within like a body endowed with soul, that is false and absurd. 5. An attribute of a body is bodily, like whiteness and blackness, which subsist in a body. But the attributes of the soul are incorporeal, such as love, hatred, sorrow, and joy. Therefore it is not a body, if bodies subsist in incorporeal things. 6. A body endowed with soul is nourished by bodily foods. But the soul is not nourished by bodily foods. Therefore it is not a body. 7. An animate body increases and decreases in length, depth, and width. But it does not increase in these dimensions; therefore it is not a body. 8. Every body, whatever it is, is in a place that contains it. Two bodies cannot be in one place. But the body and the soul are in one place. Therefore the soul is not a body. 9. No body is rational and capable of knowledge by its nature. But the soul naturally possesses reason and the capacity for knowledge. Therefore it is not a body. 10. Every

body, whatever it is, is joined to another body through contact at its boundaries. But the soul in its entirety is united with the entire body through its connection with it. Therefore it is not a body. These arguments are against those who say that the soul is a body. Against those who say that the soul is water or air. For these people say that the soul is known to be water or air because it is impossible to live without water and air. But we make two points to them. First, it is also impossible to live without food and nourishment. According to your argument, let these too be the soul. Second, there are many animals that live without drinking water, as is said of eagles and partridges. And there are many others that do not live without drawing in air, such as these segmented creatures: wasps and bees, and those that have no lungs—I mean fish, eels, and the rest. Therefore the soul is neither air nor water. Against those who say that the soul is fire. We have already demonstrated at length that the soul is incorporeal. And so we demonstrate that the soul is not fire through the following arguments. 1. Fire is a body, but the soul is not a body. Therefore

the soul is not fire. 2. Fire is perceptible to the senses, but the soul is not perceptible to the senses. Therefore the soul is not fire. 3. Whenever fire acts on a body, it burns and consumes it [?]. Therefore the soul is not fire. Against those who say that the soul is blood and breath. For they say that the soul is known to be blood and breath because, when blood and breath leave an animal, the animal dies. We say to them: If, because these things leave an animal, you have therefore said that they are the soul, then the head, brain, heart, and liver are also the soul, because when one of them, or all of them, are removed from an animal, the animal dies. Furthermore, if things are as you say, then when a portion of the blood flows away, a portion of the soul flows away. This is both absurd and false. Against those who say that the soul is a compound made of elements or of tiny bodies flying through the air. 1. A compound made of tiny bodies is a body, but the soul is incorporeal. Therefore the soul is not a compound made of tiny bodies. 2. A compound made of tiny bodies is perceptible to the senses, but the soul is not perceptible to the senses. Therefore

the soul is not a compound made of tiny bodies. A compound made of tiny bodies is composite, but the soul is simple. Therefore the soul is not a compound made of tiny flying bodies. Against those who say that the soul is not an incorporeal entity subsisting in and of itself, but subsists in something else. We speak against them in general, with God's help, in what follows, where we show that the soul is a subsistent entity. [?] After it is separated from the body, it subsists by itself and for itself, with its own distinct existence. Here, however, we speak specifically to each one of them: first, against those who say that the soul is like sight in the eyes and whiteness in snow. 1. Sight and whiteness in snow are accidents, but the soul is a substance, as we will show with God's help. Therefore the soul is not like sight in the eyes and whiteness in snow. 2. Sight in the eyes and whiteness in snow belong to the things that exist in a subject [?]. The soul, however, is a subject, and not one of the things that exist in it. For it is the subject of righteousness and wickedness, knowledge and ignorance. Therefore the soul is not like sight in the eyes

and like whiteness in snow. Against those who say that the soul is the power of the balanced mixture of the elements. 1. The power of the balanced mixture of the elements is a quality. The soul, however, is a substance, as we will show with God's help. Therefore the soul is not the power of the balanced mixture of the elements. 2. The power of the mixture is perceptible to the senses, but the soul is intelligible. Therefore the soul is not the power of the mixture. 3. The power of the balanced mixture of the elements gives health to the body. If, then, the soul is the power of the balanced mixture of the elements, a person should therefore not become sick or weak as long as he is alive and has a soul in him. Yet we see that he becomes sick and weak while he is alive and has a soul in him. 4. The balanced powers of the mixture of the elements leave the body, while the soul remains in it. Therefore the soul is not the power of the balanced mixture of the elements. If the soul is the power of the balanced mixture of the elements, 5. The power of the mixture of the elements changes according to stages of growth, ways of life, and time. Therefore the soul, too, changes

and is praised [?]. It is not one and the same soul that we have, but a different one each time, according to the changing power of the mixture of the elements: at one time that of a lion, at another that of a lamb, at another that of a wolf, and at another that of a young goat. But if this is false and absurd, the soul is not the power of the balanced mixture of the elements. 6. If the soul is the power of the balanced mixture of the elements, every body composed of elements that has the power of a mixture has a soul. Therefore every body has a soul. And if every body has a soul, then stones and iron have a soul. And things without souls turn out to have souls, which is false and absurd. Therefore the soul is not the balanced power of the elements. Against those who say that the soul is the harmony of the cohesion of the elements, using “harmony” to mean their fitting together. 1. The soul, then, often opposes the body by restraining it from its desire, or by handing it over to things that harm it. Harmony, that is, the fitting together of the elements, does not oppose the body; and if it opposes it, it is not a fitting together. Therefore the soul is not

A harmony of the blending of the elements. 2. The soul has priority and authority over the body. But the harmonious arrangement of the elements has no priority or authority over the body. Therefore, the soul is not a harmonious arrangement. 3. The soul admits justice, injustice, self-control, and virtue. But the harmonious arrangement of the elements admits none of these. Therefore, the soul is not a harmonious arrangement. 4. The soul is a substance, as we shall show with God's help. But a harmonious arrangement is a quality. Therefore, the soul is not a harmonious arrangement of the elements. 5. If the soul is a harmony, that is, a harmonious arrangement of the elements, and a harmonious arrangement is the health of the body, then a person should not become sick or weak as long as he lives and has a soul within him. For the harmonious arrangement of the elements departs from the body, but the soul remains within it even when it is sick. Therefore, the soul is not a harmony, that is, a harmonious arrangement of the blending of the elements. Against those who say that Aristotle said that the soul is the entelechy of the body. First, we say that entelechy is completion. The entelechy of something is spoken of in two ways. The first is one in which it does not govern

the thing, and when separated from it, it does not survive. An example is the shape of a ship, which is the entelechy, that is, the completion, of the ship itself; another example is the human shape, which is the entelechy of a statue. This entelechy does not survive when separated from that to which it belongs. The other kind of entelechy is something that governs a thing, and when it is separated from it—like the sailor, who is the entelechy, that is, the completion, of the ship, and also its governor. This entelechy, then, when separated from that to which it belongs, survives and subsists independently, on its own. Thus there are two ways: 1. The one that governs something survives when separated from it. 2. The other does not govern something and does not survive when separated from it. If, then, Aristotle said that the soul is the entelechy of the body in the same way that the sailor is the entelechy of the ship, that is, the completion of the ship, because it is the body's harmonious arrangement, or rather, the one that harmonizes and governs the body, he spoke well. For he is said to have

a book in which he calls the soul a rational being. But if, just as the shape of a ship is its entelechy, and the shape of a statue is the statue's entelechy, he said that the soul is the entelechy of the body, he spoke badly and very foolishly. If he spoke of the soul in this way, we bring these objections against him. 1. If the soul is the entelechy of the body, as the shape of a statue is by nature, then, when the hand of a living person is cut off, necessarily a portion of the bronze and a portion of the shape must be cut off with it. But it is clear that the soul is indivisible, as we shall show with God's help. Therefore, the soul is not the entelechy of the body in the same way that shape is the entelechy of a statue. 2. If the soul were the entelechy of the body, like the shape in a ship, it could not come into conflict with the body. And yet we see that it often opposes his passions in many ways. For he desires to eat, or to drink, or to have sexual intercourse, and it sometimes restrains him from this. Therefore the soul is not the actuality of the body. 3. If the soul were the actuality of the body, like the shape of a ship’s hull, it could not contain impressions, images, and likenesses

of physical objects when they are removed from it after it has seen them. Yet we see that it receives them and that they are preserved within it. 4. If the soul is the actuality of the body, then it receives its existence from the body, so that it exists, and the body is superior to it, because the body is the cause of its existence. Consequently, it is inferior to that from which it comes into being. But it is known and evident that the soul is superior to the body in many ways, and fills the world with knowledge, wisdom, skilled crafts, and the rest. Therefore the soul is not the actuality of the body in the way that shape is the actuality of a ship or a house. Against those who say that the soul is the exercise of the senses, a number that moves itself, or a collection of understanding and memory. (1.) The exercise of the senses, understanding, and memory are accidental properties. The soul, however, is a substance. Therefore the soul is not the exercise of the senses, number, understanding, or memory. (2.) For it belongs to the things that exist in a subject. The soul, however, is itself the subject. Therefore the soul is not exercise, number, understanding, or memory. (3.) The exercise of the senses, understanding, memory, and number do not move the body fully (rationally). Therefore the soul is not

the exercise of the senses, number, understanding, or memory. Against Plato, who said that even irrational animals have a soul. We say that irrational animals have a soul, and this is known from the following demonstrations. First: irrational animals have no rational activity at all, nor understanding, nor thought, nor writings, nor any skilled craft—things that are discoveries of the rational soul. 2. It is known that they have no rational soul from the fact that they cannot receive a law, as a rational soul can. No one has ever laid down a law for doves, donkeys, or fish requiring them to fast or pray. 3. It is known that they have no rational souls from the fact that they do not fear the punishment of the world to come, nor do they look forward to the reward that is to come or that has been promised. 4. It is also known that they have no rational soul from the fact that contrary activities are not observed in them. I mean that when they are hungry and have food, they cannot refrain from eating. Nor can they refrain when they desire to mate and find an opportunity; instead, they mate immediately, at that very moment.

And so it is with the other things as well. 5. Again, it is known that irrational animals have no rational soul from the fact that each one of them performs the very same activity characteristic of its species, even if it performs it to a greater degree, and cannot change that activity or refrain from performing it in some way. Camels are the most resentful of all; wolves are gluttonous; lions are among the brave; hares are timid; foxes are cunning; and peacocks are proud. From this it is known that they act not rationally but irrationally. 6. But if someone from the school of Plato objects and says that children too do not move rationally, we say to him: Although at the stage of childhood they do not display rational activity, at a later stage they act rationally. Irrational animals, however, do not display rational activity at any stage of their lives, but only irrational activity. But if they object again and say that their activities are rational and that they possess rational movement, but the formation of their limbs does not allow them to accommodate rational activity,

just as people whose fingers have been lost are prevented from practicing their craft, we say to them: Then, according to their argument, the Creator did not make for them a soul suited to their bodies, but one unsuited to them. If this is so, then God created the souls of irrational animals in vain. But it is false that God created anything in vain, as one of the sages said concerning created things and their coming into being: “He did not create a single one of them without purpose.” Indeed, not even a wise human being does anything in vain—how much less God! Against the Manichaeans, who say that the soul is incorporeal, is divided among individual bodies, and is immortal. If it is divided, it is not incorporeal but corporeal. For what is incorporeal does not admit division into parts at all. A body, however, is indeed divisible. By this you have contradicted your assertion that the soul is incorporeal. If the soul is divided, it is a body. And if it is a body, it is mortal, because everything that lives and is a body is mortal.

Thus you have also overturned your other assertion, which says that the soul is immortal. And if the soul is one, as you have said, and is divided among each individual body, then stones and iron, which are inanimate bodies, would be found to have a soul [?] and not to be inanimate. This is false. Therefore the soul is not as the Manichaeans suppose it to be. Demonstration that the soul is a substance. It is evident that the soul is a substance from the following demonstrations. 1. Now this is the distinctive property of a substance, as the sages understand it: that, while remaining one and the same, it can receive contrary qualities through a change in its own condition. A physical body is a substance: sometimes it is white, and sometimes black. And a living body, being a substance, is sometimes healthy and sometimes sick. Thus a physical body and a living body, which are substances, receive whiteness and blackness, health and sickness, which are contrary accidents. In the same way, the soul too, while remaining one and the same, sometimes receives righteousness and becomes

righteous, and sometimes receives injustice and becomes unjust. Likewise, at different times it receives chastity and licentiousness, which are contrary to one another. If, then, this is the distinctive property of a substance—that, as it changes from its natural condition, it receives contrary qualities in different ways— Therefore the soul is a substance. 2. It is known that the soul is a substance from the body, which is a substance. For it is not possible for what is moved, acted upon, and governed to be a substance. Therefore the body, which is moved, is a substance. The soul that moves it must necessarily also be a substance. 3. It is known that it is a substance from the teachings we learn. They do not subsist in our body. This is known from the fact that not all things that are bodies receive teachings. For irrational animals are bodily beings, yet they do not receive teachings and knowledge. The soul, however, receives teachings. And if teachings subsist in it, as an accidental property in a substance. 4. It is known that it is a substance from the fact that it is preserved and continues to exist after its release from the body, as we are going to demonstrate with God's help.

Showing that the soul is incorporeal. It is known, then, that the soul is incorporeal from these syllogisms, which are formulated in the first figures. 1. A body has three dimensions: length, depth, and breadth. The soul, however, does not have three dimensions. Therefore it is incorporeal. 2. Every body is perceptible to the senses. But the five senses do not apprehend the soul. Therefore it is incorporeal. 3. When a body is added to another body and joined to it, it adds weight to it. But the soul does not add weight to the body when it is united with it. Therefore it is [?]. 4. Incorporeal accidental properties affect the soul, such as righteousness and injustice, virtue and wickedness. But incorporeal accidental properties do not affect a body. Therefore the soul is not a body. 5. The soul is nourished by incorporeal foods—I mean teachings and knowledge. But a body is not nourished by incorporeal foods. Therefore the soul is not a body.

And a body and another body cannot be in one location and one place when united. Therefore the soul is incorporeal. 6. The soul possesses the capacity for knowledge by its nature. A body, however, does not possess the capacity for knowledge and perception by its nature. Therefore the soul is incorporeal. These other demonstrations showing that the soul is incorporeal are in the fourth chapter. These, then, are syllogisms showing that the soul is incorporeal. The testimonies from the Holy Scriptures that confirm that the soul is incorporeal are these. Our Lord says in his Gospel: “Do not fear those who kill the body, but cannot kill the soul.” First, the soul is incorporeal; second, it is immortal. It is incorporeal because it cannot be struck by a sword or undergo the sufferings that affect the body, which is corporeal. It is immortal because it is not killed as the body is killed. Again he says: “A human being will not live on bread

alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God.” By saying, then, “but on every word,” he showed that it is the soul that is nourished by words. And by its being nourished by words and teachings, he showed that it is incorporeal. And again the apostle Paul spoke about himself in this way: “I know a man in Christ. Whether in the body or without the body, I do not know. God knows that this man was caught up to the third heaven.” Now, by saying, “Whether without the body,” he showed that the soul’s nature is neither bodily nor material, but is another, immaterial nature, distinct from the nature of the body. Again he wrote to the Hebrews: “Remember those who are afflicted, as people who are yourselves clothed in flesh.” He showed that the garment, which is a body, is different from the one who wears it. It is clear that the soul, which wears the flesh, is immaterial. And again the prophet David said: “Let us hear what the Lord our God will say.” And many times the prophet [?] God speaking. And just as

his speech came forth through a physical mouth, so the prophets did not hear him with physical ears either, but with physical souls. Thus it has been shown through what has been said that the soul is immaterial. Showing that the soul is simple. Now the soul is simple, and this is clear from the following. The soul is immaterial, and everything immaterial is simple. Therefore the soul is simple. The soul is not divided or cut into parts, and everything that is not divided into parts is simple. Therefore the soul is simple. The soul is not composed of elements, and everything that is not composed of elements is simple. Therefore the soul is simple. These, then, are three syllogisms in the first figure establishing that the soul is simple. Showing what we should investigate first: the soul’s nature, its power, or its activity. We say that these are three things: nature, powers, and activities. Nature is something that subsists. Powers subsist in nature, while activities arise from powers. Therefore someone who investigates powers or activities while neglecting to investigate nature first is like a blind person who, guided by hearing alone, tries to mix colors and paint beautiful images and splendid likenesses. We should first investigate the soul’s nature, asking what it is, because it is the first thing on which examining thought rests. For it subsists in and of itself, and does not subsist in anything else at all, since it is, and is called, a substance. And afterward, also because the powers have their subsistence in nature itself, we should investigate the soul’s power, because the powers precede activities. Then we investigate the soul’s activities, because they arise from its powers. Therefore we should first investigate the soul’s nature.

Showing what the soul’s nature is. Someone rightly asks: “What is the soul’s nature?” We say that the soul’s nature is life. But if he replies, “How is it known that its nature is life?” we say that it is known from the following demonstrations. 1. Everything that lives, living by its own nature and not through something else, is alive by its own nature. Now the soul lives by its own nature and not through something else. Therefore its nature is life. 2. The body is not alive by its own nature, but lives through something else. This is clear from the fact that when the life within it departs, it is left lifeless. The soul’s nature, however, is life. And this is known from the fact that its nature never remains when it is not alive. 3. That whose nature is life does not come to an end. And the soul does not come to an end. Therefore its nature is life. And that whose nature is life does not die. And the soul does not die. Therefore its nature is life. Through these arguments it has been clearly demonstrated that the nature of the soul is life. But if someone objects and says, “If this is so, the nature of angels is also life, and consequently the nature of the soul cannot

be the nature of angels, and the nature of angels is that of the soul,” we say to him, “It is not because the nature of the soul equals the nature of angels with respect to life that the nature of angels and that of the soul must necessarily be one. For although the nature of the soul is life, one life differs from another, in that the life of angels is higher and more exalted than that of the soul. And just as one life is higher than another, so too one nature is higher and more exalted than another. Furthermore, although the nature of angels is life, they are not united with bodies. In this respect the life of angels is superior to that of the soul, and consequently their nature is likewise superior. Furthermore, the soul has properties by which its nature is distinguished from that of angels. Therefore it has been demonstrated through these arguments that the nature of the soul is life. We also say that the nature of the soul is immortal. And when we speak of immortality in relation to the soul, we indicate not a lack but a possession, as we are going to demonstrate with God's help. And what possession do we indicate when we speak of immortality in relation to

the soul? We say that it is life. Consequently, to speak of life in relation to the soul is equivalent to indicating its nature, for its nature is life. And when we say that the nature of the soul is immortality, we indicate that it is life. Likewise, when immortality is spoken of in relation to angels, it indicates life, not a lack. Therefore the nature of the soul is life. Gregory bears witness to this when he says the following in his discourse on the Nativity: “From matter he took a body, but from himself he supplied life, namely that of an intelligent soul and the image of God.” Knowledge is a term that indicates the power and activity of the soul. Now, some of the soul's powers are natural, while others are incidental. The natural ones are intellect, thought, knowledge, reason, movement, memory, and things like these. The incidental ones are anger, desire, perception through the five senses, imagination, and things like these.

1. Some of the powers of the soul are natural: intellect, thought, knowledge, reason, intrinsic movement, memory. 2. Other powers of the soul are incidental: anger, desire, perception through the five senses, imagination. These, and others like them, are the powers of the soul. But life is not known except through their activity, because they are hidden. And whatever is hidden is known through its activity. Therefore we ought to explain these powers and make them known through their activity. We describe them as follows: Intellect is the power that knows things not through words, nor through demonstrations, nor through instruction, but through direct perception.

that hidden and simple one which the saints possess in the life of souls. Reasoning is that which knows things through words, demonstrations, teachings, and syllogisms. Cognition is a power [?]. Activity is that which distinguishes true thoughts from false ones. Thus, then, the philosophers define rationality as a power that distinguishes thoughts. Self-movement is a power that moves of itself, and not through anything else. Memory is a power that gathers and preserves knowledge of teachings, since it gathers and preserves them so that they are not lost. These, then, are activities arising from the soul’s natural powers, and they make those powers known. The activities arising from the soul’s accidental powers are these: anger is that by which a person is moved to take revenge on someone who has distressed and oppressed him. Desire is that by which a person desires food, drink, sexual union,

possessions, and other such things. Sensation through the five senses is the discernment of bodily and perceptible things: colors and shapes through sight; sounds and melodies through hearing; pleasant and foul odors through smell; sweet and bitter foods and drinks, and the rest, through taste; smoothness and roughness, heat and cold, and other such things through touch. Imagination is that which generally forms false fancies, as when a person often imagines himself flying and a fish walking on land.

1. The soul’s natural powers. Intellect: that which knows things not through words, nor through demonstrations, nor through teachings, but through that hidden and simple vision. Reasoning: that which knows things through words, demonstrations, teachings, and syllogisms. Cognition: Rationality: that which distinguishes true thoughts from false ones. Self-movement: from itself, not from another. Memory: that which gathers knowledge and teachings. 2. The soul’s accidental powers. Anger: that by which a person is moved to take revenge on someone who has distressed him. Desire: that by which a person desires food, drink, sexual union, and possessions. Sensation: the discernment of bodily and perceptible things through the five senses, through sight, hearing, smell, and taste. Imagination: that which generally forms false fancies. We must therefore investigate why those powers—I mean intellect, reasoning, cognition, rationality, self-movement, and memory—are called the soul’s natural powers. Anger,

desire, sensation through the five senses, and imagination are called the soul’s accidental powers. We say that those called natural are so called for these reasons: (1) [?] because they arise from the soul’s nature and not from elsewhere. (2) Because they are naturally established in the soul’s nature. (3) Because they sustain the soul’s nature. (4) Because they are included in demonstrations concerning the soul, and through them it is distinguished from other natures. (5) Because, when they are present with the soul, they contribute to its continued existence; and if they happen to be removed from it, or even one of them is, they leave it deficient. (6) Because they belong exclusively and specifically to the soul, without the body sharing in them. But these other four— anger, desire, discernment through the five senses, and imagination—are called the soul’s accidental powers because they do not belong to the soul. Nor are they fixed and implanted in its nature; rather, they belong to the body and its constitution. Because it is joined to the body, they arise in it, and it receives them. This is because of its bond with the body. It is therefore known from the following indications that these faculties do not belong to the soul: first, because they are not included in the definitions of the soul

when it is defined. For its definition contains neither anger nor desire, nor even discrimination through the senses and through imagination. (2) Further, because the soul is created in the image of God, and these things are not in God. (3) Because holy people have overcome and conquered desire and anger. Therefore, the five senses and the four faculties do not belong to the soul, but to the body and its constitution. (4) That this is so is also known from the fact that anger and desire are found even in irrational animals. Likewise, discrimination through the five senses is also found in them, even though it is not rational discrimination. For they have discrimination through the body's five senses, but not rational discrimination of the kind human beings have. We should also investigate how these faculties arise in the soul through the body, because it is bound to the body and has its own fellowship with it. We explain it as follows: the soul itself is incorporeal, while in this world there are perceptible and visible natures, which are bodies. When it deals with them through the mediation of the body, which is corporeal, these faculties arise in it. How does this happen? We say that some bodies are distressing and others pleasant. When the soul comes into contact, through the body, with those bodies that are

distressing, it recoils from them, becomes [?] (becomes embittered), and grows angry. In this way the faculty of anger arises in it. When, through the body, it approaches those bodies that are pleasant, it finds rest, loves (loves) them, and desires them. In this way the faculty of desire arises in it. Because it deals with all bodies through the mediation of the body's five senses, that faculty which is perception through the five senses arises in it. And because imagination is generated from perception through the five senses, imagination also arises in the soul. From the things that sight, hearing, smell, and touch distinguish, a person proceeds to imagine and, for the most part, fashions false thoughts. How does this happen? From seeing an eagle flying, he imagines a donkey crawling and imagines a human being flying. From these things that are close to the senses, he imagines things that are far removed from them. Therefore, imagination is generated from perception through the five senses. Some faculties belong to the soul by nature: intellect, thought, knowledge, reason, self-movement, and memory. Other faculties belong to the body (and because it is united with the soul, they also arise in the soul): anger, desire, perception, and imagination.

Perhaps someone will object and say, ‘But in many places some of the philosophers have said that the soul has three faculties: reason, anger, and desire.’ To this we reply that, in saying that reason is a faculty of the soul, they spoke correctly. Reason is indeed a faculty of the soul, as we have shown above. But concerning the statement that anger and desire are faculties of the soul, we will give them one of two answers. Either they strayed from the truth in this and spoke falsely, or they did not stray from the truth, but you were mistaken, O author. Because the word ‘soul’ has more than one meaning, they took it in a general sense and did not distinguish its different meanings, and so went astray. Or they called them faculties of the soul, although they belong not to the soul but to the body. They also occur in the soul, and therefore are called the soul’s incidental powers, as we showed in the preceding discussions. Showing that the soul is rational and self-moving—that is, that it moves of itself and not through another.

And that it is always moving—that is, that it moves continually, never ceasing to move. It is evident, then, that the soul is rational from the fact that it distinguishes true thoughts from false thoughts. For philosophers define rationality in this way: it is the power to distinguish thoughts. If rationality is the power to distinguish thoughts, and the soul has the power to distinguish thoughts, then the soul has rationality. And if it has rationality, it is evident that it is rational. It is also evident that it is self-moving, that is, that it moves of itself, from the following arguments. First: a human being is composed of two natures [?]. And it is the soul that moves the body rationally. If, then, it is the soul that moves the body, and there is no third thing that moves it, then it moves of itself. For something that moves and also moves another, when there is no other thing moving it, itself moves of itself. (2) This is evident from the following: whatever lives of itself and not through another moves of itself and not through another. The soul, however, is life by its nature and has life from itself, not from another. Therefore it moves of itself and not through another. (3) This is evident

from the following: if the body does not move rationally of itself, but only through the soul, it is evident that the soul moves of itself and not through another, because the soul’s powers oppose those of the body, as Paul, the great apostle, says: “The spirit desires what is harmful to the body,” and likewise the reverse. If, then, the body does not move rationally of itself, the soul, however, moves of itself. The soul is also known to be always moving—that is, to move continually, never at all ceasing its movement—from the following demonstrations. 1. From the fact that it moves of itself. Whatever moves of itself does not cease its movement. The soul, however, moves of itself. Therefore it does not cease its movement, but moves continually. (2) From the fact that the body sometimes moves and sometimes ceases its movement, and the soul’s powers oppose those of the body. Therefore the soul moves continually, without ceasing its movement. (3) From the fact that a human being has two kinds of speech: one is [?] fixed within, and the other is expressed outwardly. The inward kind is born from the soul, while the outward kind is carried out through the body. And the kind

that is born from the soul is not thinking, as some have supposed and said, but is the power to distinguish thoughts. For we call this rationality—the power just mentioned—“speech that is born from the soul.” That is, this speech is neither thinking nor a thought. This is clear for two reasons. First, because this speech distinguishes true thoughts from false ones, and thoughts are distinguished by it. What distinguishes is distinct from the things distinguished by it, just as a saw is distinct from planks: the former separates, while the latter are separated. It is also evident from the fact that thoughts cut one another off and are cut off by one another. This speech, however, does not cut itself off, nor is it cut off by itself. Therefore, the speech that is born from the soul is not thought, but rationality—that is, the faculty that distinguishes thoughts. Outward speech, however, is what is heard and is produced through the body—that is, through the mouth, tongue, palate, teeth, and lips, when air enters the throat and comes out. Thus human beings have two kinds of speech, namely, one

that is born from the soul and remains within, and another that is produced through the body and is outward. Sometimes it is in motion, and sometimes it is still. But the speech that remains within is constantly in motion, never ceasing its movement. For even if someone wishes to stop its movement for a single blink of an eye, he cannot. Therefore, just as this inward speech is—is—constantly in motion, and just as outward speech is sometimes (still) and sometimes not, so too the body through which it is produced is sometimes in motion and sometimes not. Thus these things have shown that the soul is constantly in motion and moves continually. Showing in how many senses motion is spoken of, which kind of motion we say the soul has, and what the soul’s motion is, and what the definition of this motion is. Aristotle the philosopher, then, said in his book on the Categories that motion is spoken of in six senses: (two with respect to substance), two with respect to quantity, one with respect to quality, and another with respect to place. With respect to substance,

as in coming into being and destruction. Coming into being is like human seed that is sown and from which a complete human body comes into being. Destruction is like the human body that undergoes motion and is destroyed through death. With respect to quantity, there are growth and diminution. Growth is like a plant that undergoes motion and grows in size. Diminution is like a plant that is sown and decreases in size. Motion with respect to quality occurs through the alteration of a physical object or body that undergoes motion and changes from whiteness to blackness, or from blackness to whiteness. Motion with respect to place is movement from one place to another. This is divided into seven kinds: upward and downward, to the right and to the left, forward and backward, as when someone shoots an arrow or throws a stone toward one of these six directions… and circular motion, as when a millstone moves and turns in a circle.

Motion is spoken of in six senses: coming into being, like seed that becomes a body; destruction, like a body that is destroyed; growth, like a plant that grows; diminution, like a tree that diminishes; alteration, like a physical object that becomes black or white; movement from one place to another: upward, like fire that rises upward; downward, like—like water that descends downward; to the right, like an arrow that is shot; to the left; forward; backward, as toward one of these directions; circularly, like a millstone that moves. In which of these kinds of motion does the soul move? We say that it does not move by changing from one place to another, nor by growth or diminution, or by destruction, because it is only bodies that move with these kinds of motion. Bodies

grow in size and diminish; bodies move from one place to another; and bodies are destroyed. But the soul is incorporeal. Therefore it does not move in these kinds of motion. Nor does it move by the kind of motion that consists in coming into being, because it has already come into being. It is not like human seed, which moves little by little and becomes a fully formed human body. Therefore the soul does not move by these five kinds of motion, nor by any one of them. It remains, therefore, that the soul moves by the kind of motion spoken of in a general sense. That this is so is evident from the fact that this motion is described as alteration. It is spoken of both in relation to bodies and in relation to what is incorporeal. Thus, just as the body moves and changes from whiteness to blackness and from (blackness) to whiteness, so the soul also moves and changes from evil to good and from good to evil, and from fear and from joy, and from ignorance to knowledge, and from learning to forgetfulness, and from forgetfulness

to recollection. We should therefore investigate what the soul’s motion is. We say that the soul’s motion is a power: a spiritual power by which it moves continually and without pause toward knowledge and learning, and toward thoughts and the distinctions between them, and toward virtue and wickedness, courage, fear, and joy, and toward other things of this kind. We must also state what the definition of motion is. We say that the definition of motion is a passage from potentiality to activity. Take an example of this: the intellect is a power of the soul. The activity of this power is to know things, not through demonstrations and words, but through simple and hidden knowledge. Motion, therefore, is a path and a passage from this power to this activity. Understand the soul’s other powers and activities in the same way. This is shown more clearly by the division set out below: Soul. Intellect: knowing things without speech. Thought: knowing things through words. Reason: distinguishing thoughts. Showing that the soul has the capacity to think. The soul has the capacity to think. This is known from the following. 1. From the knowledge and skills that human beings have discovered, since they discovered them through the soul’s thoughts, and not by chance or at random. 2. From the fact that we first form things in our thoughts before making them, something that our bodily senses do not show us. For the carpenter first pictures a chair and its shape in his thought before making it. Likewise, the architect first pictures a house in his thought before building it. 3. It is known that the soul has the capacity to think from the fact that we cannot see the nature of things with our senses. Instead, we understand and know it through the soul’s thoughts. Therefore the soul has the capacity to think. Showing how many properties the soul has and what they are. One of the soul’s properties, then, is this: that, of all created rational beings, it alone

needs to use discerning thought and the turning over of thoughts to determine whether it should do something or not. (2) Another is that, while bound to the body, its companion and dwelling place, it contemplates and sees distant things in the imagination as though they were nearby, without moving or going far from its dwelling. (3) Another is that, when the body to which it is bound sleeps, and it too rests with it because of their mutual bond, it strives to do the things with which it was occupied while awake. (4) That, while bound to the body, it suffers with it in its sufferings and is distressed by its pains, although it is not subject to suffering by nature. (5) This means that it hates injustice and loves righteousness, even though it stumbles, goes astray, and misdirects its own faculties. (6) That it discovers various arts and diverse knowledge. Here is an indication of the soul’s powers and properties. But in the preceding section it was more appropriate

to explain what the definition of the soul is and what it is like. We therefore say that the definition of the soul is this: a living substance, immortal, intelligent, capable of thought, capable of knowledge, capable of memory, self-moving, luminous, subtle, pure, rational, invisible, which is united to the body and separates from it for a time, and [?] is united to it inseparably. By calling it a living substance [?]. The remaining terms indicate its natural powers and essential distinctions, explaining them to us through lofty contemplations. But here, along with the remaining terms, we say:

By calling it luminous, we do not mean that it has the light of the sun or of a lamp’s flame, but that it is luminous in its knowledge of events and things. By calling it subtle, we do not mean that it resembles subtle bodies, which undergo the effects of opposing forces through [?], in relation to the opposite aspect of dense bodies. Rather, it escapes those means by which the body is perceived. It is pure because its nature does not in any way admit the body’s corporeal [?]. It is rational because it has no downward inclination at all. It is invisible because it is not a body and does not possess three dimensions. By being united to a material body—that is, to the body—it differs from angels, who are not united to bodies. The soul is known more clearly from this division: the definition of the soul is a substance: “Substance”: the genus of the definition. “Living”: the soul’s nature. “Immortal”: the soul’s nature. “Intelligent”: a power of the soul. “Capable of memory”: a power of the soul. “Capable of knowledge”: a power of the soul. “Self-moving”: a power of the soul.

“Luminous”: a distinction of the soul from bodies. “Subtle”: a distinction of the soul from bodies. “Pure”: a distinction of the soul from bodies. “Light”: a distinction of the soul from bodies. “Invisible”: a distinction of the soul from bodies. “United to the body”: a distinction of the soul from bodies. Demonstration that the soul is immortal. That the soul is immortal is known with certainty from these demonstrations. 1. Everything that exists is either simple or composite. Wherever there is composition, there is also opposition. There is also conflict and struggle there. Wherever there is struggle, there is dissolution and disintegration. Wherever there is dissolution and disintegration, there is also death. But where there is simplicity, there is no composition. Where there is no composition, there is no opposition either. Where there is no opposition, there is no struggle or strife.

Where there is no struggle, there is no dissolution or disintegration. Where there is no dissolution, there is no death either. Therefore, where there is simplicity, there is no death. It is therefore known that the soul is immortal because it is simple. How so? The soul is simple, and what is simple does not die, because where there is simplicity, there is no death. 2. From the fact that it is living and constantly in motion. The soul, then, is constantly in motion and lives through motion. It does not come to an end; it does not die. Therefore the soul does not die. 3. From the fact that the soul does not sleep. For even when the body [?], it carries out its activities. For the soul does not sleep. And what does not sleep does not die. Therefore the soul does not die. Indeed, one of the teachers also said that the soul does not die because the soul does not sleep. 4. From the fact that it is life by its nature. The soul, then, is life by its nature; that is, its nature is life and does not die. Therefore the soul is immortal. 5. It is known that the soul does not die from the fact that the body dies, for it is the body's opposite. And if the body dies, the soul necessarily does not die, since it is the body's opposite. The body, then, dies, but the soul is the body's opposite. Therefore

the soul does not die. 6. It is known that it does not die from the fact that the body is sustained by its good qualities and destroyed by its bad qualities. The body's good qualities, then, are beauty, health, constitution, and soundness of its limbs. For these good qualities sustain the body. Therefore the body's good qualities sustain it. But the soul is not sustained by its good qualities, nor is it destroyed by its bad qualities. Its good qualities are righteousness, virtue, serenity, joy, and other things like these. Its bad qualities are injustice, envy, frivolity, hatred, distress, and things like these. And if the soul's good qualities do not sustain it, and its bad qualities do not destroy it, then it does not die. 7. There are three kinds of destruction. One is the dissolution of composite structures, as when the structure of a house or a ship is dissolved. Dissolution, then, destroys the house and also the ship. Another is division and cutting into parts, as when a piece of wood ten cubits long is divided and cut into parts and small pieces. In this way, division and cutting destroy it as it is cut up. Another is what happens through the transformation of something,

when it is destroyed as what it was and becomes something else, as in the case of human seed, which is destroyed as seed and becomes a body. Therefore destruction happens in three ways: 1. The dissolution of a composite structure, such as the dissolution of a house. 2. The cutting up of something, such as the division of a piece of wood. 3. The transformation of something, as when (seed) is destroyed and becomes a body. None of these three kinds of destruction, then, affects the soul. The soul does not die. 8. From the fact that it moves the body. For if the body that is moved is mortal, the soul that moves it does not die. It is known from this that it does not die: two kinds of affliction come upon a human being, one affecting the body, I mean, and the other affecting the soul. Those affecting the body are wounds, cuts, beatings, distress, pain, and things like these. Those affecting the soul are sin, guilt, wrongdoing, shortcomings,

error, or things like these. The body's afflictions—wounds, cuts, and the rest—are not kept for retribution. Therefore the body in which they exist is also dissolved. But the soul's afflictions—sin, guilt, and the rest—are kept for retribution. Therefore the soul in which they exist is neither dissolved nor dies. 9. It is known that the soul does not die from this premise: providence exists, and if providence exists, judgment necessarily exists as well. And if judgment exists, there is also someone to be judged.
