And if there is someone to be judged, an immortal soul necessarily exists as well. These demonstrations come from natural and rational inquiries, which show that the soul is immortal. The testimonies from the Holy Scriptures that confirm that the soul does not die are these: God said to Moses, “I am the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.” And God is not the God of the dead, but of the living. By saying that God is not the God of the dead but of the living, he showed that their souls are not dead but alive. And Solomon said, “The body returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit to the Lord

who gave it.” By saying that the spirit returns to the earth as the body returns [?], he showed that it is imperishable. But by saying that it returns and goes back to the Lord, he made known that it is not dead but alive. And again our Lord said in the Gospel, “Do not be afraid of those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul.” Thus, by saying that they cannot kill it, he showed two things: first, that the soul is not bodily; and second, that it is not mortal. It is not bodily because it cannot undergo the sufferings that come upon the body, which is a physical substance. It is not mortal because it is not destroyed (killed) like the body. And again he said in the account of the rich man and Lazarus that after the rich man died and was buried, the angels carried Lazarus to Abraham’s embrace, and that the rich man asked Abraham for water, and so on. Thus, by saying that the angels carried Lazarus to Abraham’s embrace, and by Abraham’s replies to the rich man, through all these things he showed that souls are alive and never

die. And again the divine apostle Paul spoke about the body in this way: “This perishable thing is destined to put on imperishability, mortality [?].” It was as though he were holding the body in his hand and pointing to it with his finger when he said, “This thing that perishes and dies.” And by saying of the body, “This thing that perishes and dies,” he showed that the soul is imperishable and does not die. Therefore the soul is immortal. Showing in what sense, when we apply these terms to the soul—“immortality,” “not bodily”— we apply them to it: as a deprivation or as a possession. There are terms which, when spoken, seem to indicate deprivation, although they indicate not deprivation but possession. And again there are terms which, when spoken, seem to indicate possession, although they indicate not possession but deprivation. How is this so? Those which seem to indicate deprivation, although they indicate not deprivation but possession, are these: “bodiless,” “irrational,” “immortal,” “soulless,”

and others like these. But those which seem to indicate possession, although they indicate not possession but deprivation, are these: sickness, nakedness, poverty, blindness, evil, darkness, and others like these. Sickness is deprivation of health; nakedness is deprivation of clothing; poverty is deprivation of wealth; blindness is deprivation of sight; darkness is deprivation of light; and evil is deprivation of goodness. But those privative terms—I mean “bodiless,” “immortal,” “irrational,” “soulless,” and others like them—indicate two things: both what is inferior to that of which it is the deprivation, and what is superior to it. How is this so? When we say “bodiless,” we have not simply expressed a deprivation; rather, we have indicated one of two things. Or something inferior to a body, such as matter alone, or form alone, or such things as qualities and modes. For all these

are incorporeal because they are inferior to bodies. Or, when we say “incorporeal,” we signify something superior to bodies, as in the case of angels and souls: they are incorporeal because they are superior to bodies. Thus “incorporeal” does not signify a privation, but a positive property that is either inferior to that from which the privation is derived or superior to it in this way. The same applies to “immortal.” When we say “immortal,” we do not signify a privation, but two positive properties. One applies to stones and pieces of wood, which are inferior to a human being, who is immortal. The other applies to an angel or a soul, which is superior to a human being, who is mortal, the one from whom the privation is derived. It is therefore in this same way that we also say “irrational” and “soulless.” Thus it has been shown that when we call the soul immortal and incorporeal, we do not deprive it of anything by these names. Rather, we signify a positive property. For when we call it immortal, we signify that it is life. For its nature is life, as we have shown above. And when we call it incorporeal, we signify that it is superior to a body. Therefore these names, “immortal” and “incorporeal,”

when we apply them to the soul, signify a positive property, not a privation. Showing that the soul cannot be cut or divided into parts

The soul cannot be cut or divided into parts. This is evident from the following. 1. The soul is incorporeal, and what is incorporeal cannot be cut or divided into parts. It is a body that can be cut and divided into parts. Therefore the soul cannot be cut or divided into parts. 2. For just as the soul does not become paralyzed along with bodies whose hands and feet are paralyzed, nor become blind along with blind bodies, or deaf or [?] along with deaf and [?] bodies, so it is not cut along with hands and feet that are cut off, or along with other bodily members that are cut off. Therefore the soul cannot be cut or divided into parts. But if someone objects and says, “If [?] the soul is not cut along with the members when a member is cut off, why does it twitch, stir, and move after being cut off?” We say that the severed member experiences this, not because the rational soul was cut off along with it, but because the power of sensation and movement, which irrational animals and bodies possess, was cut off along with it.

Showing that the soul governs the body

Someone asks, “Which governs the other, and which is governed by the other? Does the soul govern the body, or does the body govern the soul?” We say that it is the soul that governs the body. This is evident from the following demonstrations. 1. From the fact that the body is its instrument, through which it does good and evil, and through which it acts righteously and sins. Whoever works with an instrument governs that instrument. Therefore the soul governs the body. 2. It is evident that the soul governs the body from the fact that it often restrains it from its desire. For there are times when the body desires to eat, drink, sleep, and have sexual intercourse. And it restrains it from its desire. Sometimes people's bodies are gripped by burning fevers, and they long for a cold drink. Because it would harm them, the rational soul prevents them from drinking. Therefore, it is the soul that governs the body. 3. Often, when a craftsman has set himself a goal, he misses it and then goes back and puts things right somehow. Sometimes, when an architect has set himself the goal of raising a house ten cubits high, he raises it twelve. This happened because the soul's thought did not keep pace with the body's movement, nor did the soul's rational faculty restrain

the body's movement toward building twelve cubits high. Consequently, he missed his goal, and not [?]. Then he goes back and repairs what he spoiled, using the very same body and the very same hands. From these things it is clear that the soul governs the body. 4. During the movement of contemplation, the body is still. When contemplation is complete, the body then brings it out through action corresponding to the movement of contemplation. And since contemplation is an activity of the soul, action takes place through contemplation. Therefore, it is indeed the soul that governs the body. 5. Paul, the great apostle, says, “I discipline my body and bring it into subjection.” He showed three things in this statement. First, that Paul himself, in his own person, is a soul. Second, that his body is an instrument of his soul, since he calls it “my body.” Third, that his soul governed the body. For he did not say, “My body disciplines itself,” or, “It governs itself,” but, “I”—that is, I who am a soul—“discipline my body and bring it into subjection.” And if the soul disciplines and subjects, while the body is disciplined and subjected, then the soul governs the body, as the truthful and divine apostle said,

Paul. Truly, then, the soul enables the body to move, to act rationally, and to live rationally. Showing in how many ways anything that differs from something else is said to differ, and whether souls differ from one another or do not differ, and by what difference souls differ from one another. Anything that differs from something else either differs from it in itself, or differs from it by some other difference. What differs in itself differs from its counterpart, as in the case of whiteness and blackness. Whiteness differs in itself from blackness. That is, in what it is, it differs from white. But something that differs from its counterpart by a difference other than the things that differ through it is spoken of in many ways. This difference, then, is either essential, accidental, or individual. Essential difference is, for example, rationality and irrationality. For a human differs from a donkey by rationality. Likewise, a donkey differs from a human by irrationality. Accidental difference, however, is spoken of in two ways: an accident is either changeable or unchangeable. A changeable accident

is, for example, standing and sitting, or movement and rest. For Socrates differs from Plato because the former is standing and the latter is sitting; Socrates is moving, while Plato is still. An unchangeable accident is, for example, being blue-eyed or snub-nosed. Anytus, who is blue-eyed, differs from Meletus, who is (is not) blue-eyed. And Meletus, who is snub-nosed, differs from Anytus, who is not snub-nosed. Individual difference consists of the distinguishing properties of the individual. These properties are living, characterizing, and distinctive, such as being unbegotten, which is Adam’s distinctive property. And proceeding, which is Eve’s distinctive property. For Adam differs from Eve in being begotten, and Eve differs from Adam and Seth in proceeding. For God created Adam and brought him into existence without his being begotten. He created Eve and brought her into existence by procession from Adam’s rib, bringing her out of his side. And God created Seth and brought him into existence by birth from Adam and Eve. These kinds of differences can be understood from the division drawn below. Just as smoothness differs in itself from roughness, and just as thought differs in itself—that is, in what it is.

Everything that differs from another, or differs from it in itself, is either substantial, as in the case of mortality and immortality— for a human being differs from an angel in mortality, and likewise an angel differs from a human being in immortality— or accidental: either changeable, as in the case of silence and speech—for Socrates, who is speaking, differs from Plato, who is silent, and Plato, who is silent, differs from Socrates, who is speaking— or unchangeable, as in the case of baldness or a scar resulting from an ulcer. Anytus, who is bald, differs from Meletus, who is not bald; and Meletus, who has a scar, differs from Anytus, who has no scar. Or it is individual: As in the case of characterizing and distinctive properties: Adam differs from Seth in being unbegotten, and Seth differs from Adam and Eve in being begotten. Likewise, Eve differs from both of them in proceeding.

Let us now investigate souls: whether they differ from one another or do not differ from one another. 1. Souls are many, and things that are many differ from one another. If souls do not differ from one another, they are said to be one and not many. But the claim that they are one is false, and the claim that they are many is true. Therefore, if they are many, they are all different. 2. If they do not differ from one another, Peter’s soul is not distinct from Paul’s, nor is Socrates’ soul distinct from Plato’s. And if they do not differ and are not distinct from one another, there is great confusion. Therefore souls differ from one another. By what difference do they differ from one another? We say that they do not differ from one another by a substantial difference, because they are all rational and immortal. Their substantial powers are also equal to one another, and they do not differ in these. For they are all [?], capable of knowing, discerning, remembering, and moving themselves. Likewise, in their other natural powers too, they are equal to one another and do not differ. Therefore souls do not differ from one another by a substantial difference, nor by another difference external to themselves.

Likewise, souls too differ from one another in themselves, and not by other differences external to them. Therefore souls differ from one another in themselves—that is, in what they are—just as angels differ from one another in themselves. We also say that they differ from one another in number, in that one is the first, this one the second, another the third, another the fourth, and so on. Showing whether souls, when they depart from the body, acquire another distinction besides the one we have mentioned—that they differ from one another numerically—or not. We have shown that souls differ from one another, also numerically, just as angels differ from one another, and just as thoughts, concepts, ideas, and visions differ from one another. Someone may ask: When souls depart from bodies, do they acquire another distinction besides this one, or not? We say that they do, since, when they depart from their bodies, each one of them comes to be in spiritual places suited to their nature. Consequently, they also differ from one another by another

distinction: in attributes—I mean nonphysical ones—namely, the righteousness and wickedness they practiced here. For just as nonphysical attributes, namely whiteness, blackness, grayness, blueness, and other things like these, subsist in bodies, which are physical, so righteousness and wickedness, which are nonphysical attributes, subsist in souls, which are nonphysical. Thus, when souls depart from bodies, they come to differ from one another in two additional respects: I mean in spiritual location and also in nonphysical attributes, namely righteousness and wickedness. Consequently, we say that while souls are in bodies, they differ from one another numerically as well. And when they depart from bodies, they come to differ either in their locations or in righteousness and wickedness. Thus, when they depart from bodies, they differ from one another in four respects: number, location, righteousness, and wickedness. For example, the soul of Peter the apostle and that of Simon the magician differ from one another in that the essence of the one is different from

the essence of the other. They also differ numerically, since the one is one and the other is a second. They also differ in location, because Peter’s soul dwells with the angels, but Simon’s with the demons, until the day of the resurrection. They also differ in nonphysical attributes, because the one is righteous and holy, while the other is unjust and wicked. An inquiry concerning the souls joined to the flesh of those who were miscarried before they had taken on a recognizable form or developed all their limbs. Someone asks about the souls joined to the flesh of those who were miscarried and came out of the womb before they had taken on a recognizable form or developed all their limbs, and whose souls were released and separated from them: Are these souls like the souls that remained with bodies until childhood, youth, or old age? Or are they different and distinct from them? We say that they are like them in every respect: in nature, in being nonphysical and immortal, in their other natural powers, and in the distinctions they possess. They are like them, except in this one respect: they differ

from them in that they have no record of doing good or evil, and they do not remember having done anything here. Understand the same also concerning the souls of infants, when they and their bodies are separated from one another in infancy. Concerning where the soul comes from. Someone here asks [?], saying: Where does the soul come from? We say to him that Mani, Marcion, Bardaisan, and others with them say that the soul comes from God’s nature—that is, it is a portion of his being. Others say that a soul is born from a soul, is transmitted, and passes on. Others say that the soul is born and transmitted from the man’s seed. Where does the soul come from? Mani, Marcion, and Bardaisan say that it comes from God's nature. Others say that a soul is born from a soul and is transmitted and flows from it. Others say that it is transmitted and born from a man's seed. First, we speak against those who say that it comes from

God's nature. But it is not true that the soul comes from God's nature. This is evident from the following proofs. 1. God's nature is unchangeable, but the soul changes between righteousness and wickedness, joy and distress. Therefore, the soul does not come from God's nature. 2. The soul exists by God's will. But of God's nature it is not said that it exists by God's will, nor that it exists apart from God's will. Rather, because it is his nature, it is said to exist. Therefore, the soul does not come from God's nature. 3. The soul receives instruction and learns. God's nature does not receive instruction, because it is perfect in every respect and lacks nothing. 4. The soul has no foreknowledge. Therefore, the soul does not come from God's nature. 5. Moses said that God formed Adam and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life. Now, someone who blows does not blow out of his own nature. Rather, it is air that he draws in and that is held within him, and he brings it into his lungs and thus blows it into what is being inflated. How much more, then, did God the Creator not breathe out of his own nature when he breathed into Adam! Nor did he draw in air and blow it out as we do, for he is not bodily and is above bodily organs

and blowing. Therefore, the soul does not come from God's nature. 6. Again, it is evident that the soul does not come from God's nature from the way this leads to absurdity. Thus, if the soul comes from God's nature, and the soul is cut off from him and dwells in the body, then God's nature is divisible. 7. If the soul comes from God's nature, and there are many souls, then God's nature has many parts. 8. If the soul comes from God's nature, and the soul is different, then God's nature itself is different from it. And if that is so, it is composite. And if it is composite, it is created. 9. If the soul comes from God's nature, and the soul sins in thought and is judged, then it is God himself who sins, and God himself who judges. It follows that he sins against himself and judges, condemns, and torments himself. These are absurd things to think about God. Therefore, these arguments have shown that the soul does not come from God's nature. These arguments are against those who say that the soul comes from God's nature. Against those who say that the soul comes from a soul, and is born from it, flows from it, and is transmitted from it. That this is not true is evident from the following. 1. If, then, a body flows from a body, is born from it, and is transmitted from it,

as for the soul, which is without a body, we say that a soul is never born from a soul, nor is it transmitted or flows from it. This is evident from the following. If, then, a body flows from a body, is born from it, and is transmitted from it, the soul, which is without a body, cannot flow from, be born from, or be transmitted from another soul without a body, because the soul is the opposite of the body, just as the body is the opposite of what is without a body. Therefore, a body is born from a body, but a soul is never born from a soul. 2. It is clear, then, that what is incorporeal is not propagated from what is incorporeal, as is evident from angels and demons, who do not produce offspring. Likewise, a soul is not born from a soul. 3. The soul is simple and is not divided into parts. What is simple and is not divided into parts does not beget, nor is it born. Therefore, a soul is not born from a soul, nor is it propagated from one. But if someone objects and says, “Look, God the Father is simple and does not admit division into parts, yet he begot the Son and brought forth the Spirit,” we say to him that God the Father eternally and by nature begot the Son and brought forth the Spirit, and not through a flow and a transmission, one after another. This cannot happen with an incorporeal nature, but only with bodies. 4. If the soul is born from [?] and propagated, then it is mortal

and is subject to corruption, just as bodies are subject to it: they are born from bodies and produce offspring from themselves. Therefore, a soul is not born from a soul. These arguments, too, are against those who say that a soul is born and propagated from a soul. As for those who say that the soul is born and propagated from a man's seed, we say that this is not true. This is clear from the following arguments. 1. If the soul is incorporeal, it cannot be born from a man's seed, which is corporeal. If what is incorporeal is not born from what is incorporeal, neither is it born from what is corporeal. 2. If a man's seed is the cause and producer of the soul, and the soul is incorporeal, then a man's seed is incorporeal—which is false. Therefore, the soul does not come from a man's seed, nor is it born or propagated from it. It has therefore been clearly demonstrated by all these arguments that the soul does not come from God's nature, nor is it born or propagated from another soul, nor is it born from a man's seed. But then, where does the soul come from? We say that God created it from nothing. That he did not create it from anything is clear from the following arguments. 1. The corporeal and the incorporeal are opposites. If God created the body, which is corporeal, from something, then, because

the soul is the opposite of what is corporeal, God created it from nothing, since it is incorporeal. 2. Just as he created angels from nothing, so he also created souls from nothing and continues to create them. 3. For just as Adam's body, which he created from something— I mean, from human seed—and just as he created Adam's soul from nothing, so too he creates from nothing all the souls that come after Adam's soul, until the end of the world. For Adam's soul is also equal in nature to the souls that come afterward. 4. That God created souls from nothing is clear from the words of Zechariah, who said this about God: “He created the human spirit within him.” It is created, as the prophet said; clearly, he created it from nothing. For whatever is created is created from nothing. Our Lord also said in the Gospel: “(My Father) is working until now, and I too am working.” By saying, “I too am working,” he therefore indicated three things. The first is that he creates everything at every hour and every day, and while he creates [?] equal in nature to those that have been created. And therefore he continually creates souls today out of nothing. This is one sense of what he said:

“I too am working.” Another is that he cares for his creation in winter and summer, in sowing and harvest, giving life and putting to death, and so forth. The third sense is that he preserves his creatures. An inquiry into how the soul is created: inside the body or outside the body.
Now, since we have shown in the preceding chapter that the soul is created out of nothing, let us now investigate where the Lord creates the soul: inside the body or outside it. We say that some maintain that he creates it inside the body. This is evident from three things. The first is

that if he had created it outside the body and then brought it inside and united it with the body, it ought to remember its nature when it existed without a body, and the conditions in which it existed before entering it. Yet we see that it remembers nothing of the kind. Secondly, if he had created it outside the body and brought it inside, it would not have [?] love and harmony with it, because it would see its own loftiness and superiority, and the body's lowliness and inferiority. Consequently, one of two things would happen to it: either it would not enter the body at all, or it would simply have no love for it, but would also have hatred toward it. Yet we see that it has love and harmony with it. Thirdly, this is evident from the words of the prophet Zechariah, who spoke about God as follows: “He creates the human spirit within him.” The prophet said that he creates it. Thus, they say, our statement is true: God creates the soul within the human being. This, then, is what some have thought and said about where the soul is created. But the Greek teachers say that God creates the soul outside the body, brings it into the body, and unites it with it. Testimonies of the teachers concerning this chapter and the preceding one, showing that the soul is created out of nothing, and that God creates it outside the body and brings it into the body: Saint Severus, then, in his letter to Peter the monk, who maintained that the soul is perishable and derives its existence from seed, says the following: Severus: As for what you said, while taking pains to show that the soul is perishable and derives its existence from seed, “It is sown together with the body,” you brought forward Julian's demonstration, in which he said, “From the will of a man he called [?], and from the will of a man the inner human being is breathed into life and lives, as the material depositing of the seed imparts power to the composite being that receives it.” Know that he did not say that the soul derives its existence from the material of the seed, but that, together with the depositing of the seed, the soul is also created. Gregory of Nyssa likewise said in the third chapter of On the Formation of the Human Being that neither precedes the other, but that it has its existence in the very process of the depositing of the seed [?]. And Cyril, in what he wrote against Diodore, said that the soul and body keep pace with one another in relation to the human mind. But that the soul is complete

and is introduced from outside, and soon draws the conceived being into its own activity, Gregory the Theologian shows in his discourse in verse: “The body, for its part, is from a body.” But the soul is invisibly mingled with the form fashioned from earth (seed), entering it from outside. These things, then, are sufficient to show that parents are the cause of the body alone, and not of the soul. And that the soul is immortal: it enters from outside along with, or rather upon, the deposited seed, in a manner known to God who made it. Our soul was made from the divine breath and mingled with the body, and it is immortal and indissoluble. For dissolution is a property of the soul of an animal. It has therefore been shown that parents are the cause of the body alone. The soul, however, receives its existence from the divine breath. But because Peter the monk said that Cyril contradicted the Theologian, in that Cyril said that the breath which Moses said God breathed into Adam is the Holy Spirit, whereas the Theologian said that this breath is the soul, Saint Severus addressed him in that very same letter,

above the passages we have transcribed, as follows: He said, “Cyril says that God made a body from earth and animated it with a rational and intelligent soul in a manner known to him. And because it was fitting that it should share in the Holy Spirit, he breathed into it the breath of life. This is the Spirit who is given to creatures and fashions their likeness according to the divine likeness. And again, in the third and fourth discourse, he says: ‘The divine breath—but we do not say that it is the soul, for the soul would then have remained unchangeable, since it came forth from God. Rather, it is participation in the Holy Spirit, which was placed from the beginning in the divine soul. For this reason the rational living being came to be in the image of God. For it was to renew this that Christ breathed upon his disciples.’ Gregory the Theologian, however, said that the soul itself passed from nonexistence into existence through the breathing, and that spiritual grace was at the same time placed in the living being. ‘In it,’ he says, ‘we live and move and exist,’ as the twofold power of the breathing and the breath

that are breathed, and those who [?] the Holy Spirit. And again, in the discourse on the Nativity, he says: ‘He took matter from the body, but from himself he supplied life, namely, an intelligent soul and the image of God.’ The meaning is clear: that the human soul received its existence from the breath of God. Consider that Cyril said that he breathed into the soul so that it might receive the Holy Spirit, whereas Gregory said that the breath itself became the soul.” Peter the monk said this, and Saint Severus addressed him as follows: “Understand that those who questioned Cyril supposed that the breath itself was transformed and became a human being, rather than that the human being was created by the breath, as though by hands. To counter their ignorance, he said that the breath did not become the soul, lest they attribute change, effusion, or suffering to the whole divine essence. Rather, the soul came into being from the breath; that is, the Spirit made the soul just as he made the heavenly powers. Thus Gregory said that the power of the breathing is twofold, since it gave both breath and the Holy Spirit. Cyril, however, said that it fashioned the soul in the image,

as he contended against their error. They are therefore not in contradiction.” These passages we have brought forward from Saint Severus. Saint Cyril, however, said this: “A mother gives birth only to flesh, but God creates the rational soul, as the prophet said: ‘He creates the human spirit within him.’” But because of the natural and hypostatic union that the soul has with the body, the mother is said to give birth to the whole human being. Saint Philoxenus, who is a Syriac teacher, also said in the fifth discourse: “In the case of every woman, the flesh of the one who is born comes from her flesh, and not from her soul, just as the body of the one born of the Virgin comes from her, and not his divinity.” Theodoret of Cyrrhus also said in his book Against the Pagans: “From the bodies of existing things he fashioned the bodies of animals, and from nothing, the souls of all animals, except that of the human being alone.” These are the testimonies of the teachers, which demonstrate three things. First, that the soul is created from nothing at the Creator’s command. Second, that it is created outside the body and then enters bodies. Third, that parents bring forth only the body. Showing

whether the soul is created before the body, with the body, or after the body. Here too the questioner asks, as he investigates the soul, when it is created: before the body, together with the body, or after the body. We say that the ancient pagans, Origen, the heretics, and others with them say that souls were created beforehand, before bodies, and that because they departed from divine service, they were cast into the flesh as into a prison. But the Syriac teachers—I mean Mar Ephrem, Mar Jacob of Batnan, Philoxenus of Mabbug, and Theodoret of Cyrrhus, and the followers of Nestorius—all these say that bodies are formed first, and afterward souls are created within them from nothing. The Greek teachers, however, reject both these opinions and say that the soul does not precede the body, nor does the body precede the soul. Rather, they come together simultaneously, at the same moment, without any interval of time. The body is constituted from the man’s seed, while the soul is created suddenly from nothing at the Creator’s command. When is the soul created? Before the body, say the pagans. After the body, say the Syriac teachers. Together with the body, say the Greek teachers, both at once and simultaneously.

Let us therefore bring forward the words of Philoxenus, who is a Syriac teacher. He said in his book interpreting the Gospel: “First the body is created and takes shape in all its members, and then the soul is created within it from nothing: in a male, at forty days, and in a female, at eighty days. Therefore, also in Scripture, to make this known [?], he said in one passage: “He commanded the woman who had given birth to a male to remain forty days in the blood of purification, as one who throughout all those days had been carrying a dead body without a soul.” And again, in another passage: “If two men strike a pregnant woman and cause her child to come out, if there is a fatal injury, he shall certainly pay. But if there is no fatal injury, he shall certainly be fined whatever the woman’s husband imposes on him.” The expression “if there is a fatal injury” refers to the capacity for movement that comes to the body when the soul is created. But the expression “there is no fatal injury” refers to the child’s not yet moving at all through the soul. He has already committed murder and destroyed a human being; he too shall certainly be put to death. But if there was not yet movement through the soul, The murderer has not killed a living, rational human being, but only a dead body, or a soulless one [?]. And if the soul existed first, [?] its house, the body,

Moses would not have said that God formed dust and then [?] breathed into his nostrils. Nor, again, would Zechariah have said, “He created the human spirit within him.” These words belong to Philoxenus, who shows that the body is formed first, and afterward the soul is created within it at the Creator’s command. Mar Ephrem and Mar Jacob of Serugh likewise say the same thing in many places. So too do Theodoret of Cyrrhus and Nestorius the heretic. The Greek teachers, however, say that the soul does not precede the body, nor does the body precede the soul. Rather, they come together into unity simultaneously, as the body is formed from matter. Gregory the Theologian says this in his discourse on the Gospel passage: “I fear that some improper idea may enter, such as the notion that the soul descended elsewhere and was afterward bound in a body, and that because of their conduct there, some were assigned prophecy, while others were condemned for having behaved wickedly. But since making use of this idea is very disgraceful and contrary to the Church, let others be caught in such teaching. For us, however, being caught in such things is no mark of caution.” Gregory of Nyssa says this in his discourse On the Making of the Human Being: “Some have approved the teaching circulated concerning ‘principles’ [?], and posit souls as a certain kind of nature

in a dwelling of their own. They also place before them there examples of wickedness and virtue. As long as the soul remains in goodness, it does not experience entanglement with a body. But if it slips away from participation in goodness, it slips into life here and into a body. And because they say that it existed before the body, they say that it came into the body as into confinement in a prison. Others, following Moses’ account of the making of the human being, say that the soul comes second to our body in time, when it was formed with the body [?], and afterward the soul came through the breathing-in. They say that the soul came into being for the body’s sake, so that it might move. But everything that comes into being for the sake of something else— as the Gospel says, the soul is more important than food, and the body than clothing. Because of the matter involved in both these opinions [?], the argument is open to criticism. We say that the soul does not precede the body, nor does the body precede the soul. Rather, just as we say that a grain of wheat potentially contains the entire form of the ear—straw, stalk, grain, and husk— we do not say that any one of these precedes another in the general constitution of its nature, or that it was subsequently added to the nature of the seed. Rather, through an orderly natural process [?], the power placed within the seed is revealed. No other nature is added from outside. In the same way,

when human seed is sown, from the very first cause of its existence the power of nature unfolds and is revealed, developing through the natural sequence that brings it to completion. ‘Its own as its own, from it as from it’ is said [?]. Those who have stood up in defense of that former view and teach that the soul’s way of life is older than the powers in the body do not seem to me to be free of pagan teaching. For this reason they resemble the pagans. For if someone examines these matters carefully, he finds that their argument inevitably slips into the claim that one of their wise men said that he himself had been clothed in a woman’s body and had flown with the birds. And he brought forth trees, and living creatures in the waters came into being for him. Now Saint Cyril, in his commentary on the Gospel of John, where he takes up for examination the verse that says: “He who enlightens every person who comes into the world,” firmly established this confession through a series of very powerful arguments: souls do not precede bodies, nor do bodies precede souls. Now Andronicus, bishop of Gangra, in the book entitled The Poverty of Knowledge Falsely So Called, says as follows: “Indeed, he himself has sufficiently—

the Lord—taught that souls not only continue without passing away, but that the very same form of the body, by which they are bounded, is also preserved, and that they remember the deeds they performed here, through what he left in the account of the rich man and Lazarus, who rested in Abraham’s bosom.” Saint Severus says as follows in his letter to Simus [?]: “In the formation of a human being, the rational soul is not created first, before the body, nor is the body formed before the soul. But some people say that, because Scripture says, ‘God formed Adam,’ and afterward breathed into him, formation apparently comes first, while ensoulment comes second in order. But understand that Scripture relates these divine things in human words. It cannot recount everything all at once, and because of the inadequacy of words it cannot show or comprehend the inadequacy [?] of acts that are beyond all matter and speech. But understand that the first command and impulse of the will constitute the completion of what is being created. And we find Scripture itself speaking of everything together, in language adapted to us, to Job: ‘Or did you also take clay from the earth, form a rational living creature, and place it on the earth?’ By these words it showed that ensoulment proceeds simultaneously with formation. Thus the divine breathing brought the human soul into being.”

Again, the holy Jacob of Edessa says as follows in his letter to John of Litarba: “At present, that is, my opinion is definitely that the soul does not precede the body in its creation, nor, again, does the body precede the soul. For I judge it utterly unacceptable for anyone to think anything of this sort, and outside our fold. Both these positions are unacceptable heresies: the one that says souls precede bodies, as the pagans hold, and the one that bodies precede souls and that souls were created for their sake. Rather, by a simple command, bodies and souls were created together and are created together. However, we should know that the soul has three powers, or rather, as it were, three kinds of soul. One nourishes and promotes growth; this is also called the vegetative soul. Another senses and moves; this is also called the elemental, that is, the animal soul. The other reasons and thinks; we call it the human soul, made in God’s image. Therefore, when we say that all these three powers, or kinds, are present in the human soul, or rather, that it is all these—namely, the power of growth and nourishment, the power of sensation and movement, and rational, thinking life—if there are some among the teachers,

whether Greek or Syriac, who, considering the differences between these three powers, or kinds of souls, have said that the activity of these powers becomes manifest gradually, little by little, as though in a certain order: the vegetative power that promotes growth at the depositing of the seed; a little after it, the power of sensation and movement; and immediately after this, the power of reason and thought, shortly before birth and progressively after birth—they called this gradual sequence, this coming before and after, and this manifestation of these powers, ‘soul.’ This is also the judgment Scripture gives concerning those who strike pregnant women during a quarrel: if it is formed, he must pay the price of a life. But if it is not, he must pay a proportionate penalty. As for whether it is formed or not [?], the sages say that this falls within the count of forty. These, then, are the statements of the teachers—I mean the Syrian and Greek teachers. Some of them say that the body is formed first, and afterward a soul is created in it out of nothing. Others say that the body is formed and a soul is created in it out of nothing together, at the same time, neither preceding the other nor following the other. Rather, both proceed together, at the same time, toward union, the body being formed from seed, but the soul from nothing. We agree with and follow those Greek teachers who say that the body is formed and a soul is created in it together, at the same time. We also add our support to their position and offer proofs that this view is true. First, we speak against those who have said that the soul is created before the body. For it was not only the pagans of old who said this, but also certain people in our own time who are called Christians, though they are heretics. These people claim to demonstrate from three arguments that the soul is created before the body. Their first argument is this: They say, “Moses said that God created this creation in six days and completed it on the sixth day, and from that day onward he created nothing. If, then, the statement that God finished on the sixth day all the works he had made is true, and after their completion there is nothing else, it is clear that he did not create souls after that sixth day. Therefore, souls were created beforehand, before bodies.” We refute this argument of theirs as follows: as for Moses’ statement, “On the sixth day God finished all the works he had made,” its meaning is that he completed all the creatures he created on that

sixth day, and from then onward he did not create another kind of creature that he had not created in the six days. For if the souls he creates today were new creatures that had not been created in the six days, Moses’ statement that God finished on the sixth day the works he had made would be proved false. But the souls he creates today are not new creatures, since on that very sixth day he created Adam’s soul and Eve’s soul, which are the same in nature as the souls he creates today. Because he created them on that very sixth day, Moses’ statement that God finished on the sixth day the works he had made is confirmed and stands true, since after that sixth day he did not create a new kind of creature that had not already been created. Our statement that he continually creates souls today also stands true, because they are not a kind of creature that was not created in the six days. Therefore, souls are not created before bodies. Moreover, that God creates souls today is established by the words of the prophet Zechariah, who said, “He creates the human spirit within a person.” By saying “creates,” he indicated that God continually creates human spirits. It is also clear that he creates souls today from the words of the Lord, who said, “My Father, to this day,

works, and so do I.” By saying “I work,” he indicated three meanings: the first is that he continually creates souls. The second is that he cares for his creatures and governs them in winter or summer, in sowing and harvest, through the rains he sends down and the rivers he makes flow. He gives life and puts to death, and so on. The third is that he preserves them so that they do not perish. The second argument is this: They say, “In the beginning God created the creation from nothing; today he creates creatures from something: a human being from a human being, a horse from a horse, and gnats from decay, and so on. And if in the beginning he created creatures from nothing, but today creates them from something, and souls belong among the creatures created from nothing, then they were created in the beginning, and their creation preceded that of bodies.” For God did not create all the creatures he created in the beginning from nothing. Some he created from nothing, and some from something. Those he created from nothing are earth, water, air, fire, and souls. Those he created from something are these: the firmament, birds, creeping things, livestock, trees, grass, and so on. We have learned these things from the holy Scripture of blessed Moses. Thus, in the beginning he created some creatures from nothing, and some

from something. This is the correct formulation: Just as in the beginning he created creatures from nothing, and some from something, so also today he creates some creatures from nothing—I mean souls— and some from something—I mean the bodies of human beings and irrational animals, and so on. Their third argument is this: A human being is composed of four elements and a rational soul. “Just as the elements already exist before the human being is put together, so too the soul—the soul precedes the body,” they say. Refutation: Your analogy does not hold: that just as the elements precede the human being’s composition, so too does the rational soul. Rather, a human being is composed of a body made from four elements and a rational soul. It follows, then, that we should draw this conclusion: Just as the body does not precede the human being’s composition, neither does the rational soul. Rather, a human being is composed of a body made from four elements and a rational soul. It follows, then, that we should draw this conclusion: Just as the body does not precede the human being’s composition, neither does the rational soul precede his composition. Therefore this analogy supports our argument, not yours. Thus the soul does not precede the body in its creation. Again we say to them: If the soul had existed earlier and had been created before the body, it ought to remember itself from before

it was brought into the body, how it existed, and in what condition it was placed. For it has the capacity to remember, and memory is one of its natural powers. Yet we see and understand that it remembers nothing of this sort. Therefore the soul does not precede the body in creation. Again we say: If it had existed earlier and was afterward brought to the body with which it was united, one of two things would have happened to it: either it would not have entered it at all, considering its own rationality and the glory of its nature, and the lowliness and baseness of the body’s nature, or it would have entered it by force, and would have had not friendship and harmony with it, but hatred and discord. And indeed we see that the soul loves the body, is in harmony with it, and is drawn toward its desires for the most part. Thus these things show that the soul does not precede the body in its creation. Others, in turn, say that the body is formed first, and afterward the soul is created within it. They too, through their arguments, confirm this view of ours. They say, “It is clear that this is true because the law did not prescribe a death sentence for someone who strikes a woman and causes her to miscarry before the child has developed its shape and limbs, because the soul is not united with it while it has not yet developed its shape

and limbs, since the law did not prescribe a death sentence for him.” But this was not the reason. For the soul was united with it at the very depositing of the seed. Rather, it was because the body that was miscarried had not yet developed its shape and limbs and was not distinguishable from that of irrational animals that there was no death sentence for him. Once it had developed its shape and limbs, and was thereby distinguishable from that of irrational animals, the law prescribed a death sentence for anyone who destroyed it. That this is so is clear from the fact that killing affects the body, not the soul, according to the Lord’s statement: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul.” Thus the body does not precede the soul in its formation. Their second argument is this: they say, “It is clear that the body precedes the soul in its formation because blessed Moses said of God that he formed the dust first, and afterward breathed into it the breath of life.” We reply to them that the prophet Moses was recounting divine deeds in human words. There, in an instant, you formed the dust, created the soul, and breathed it into it, all at once, beyond our perception, understanding, and speech. And when Moses wished to express this

divine and instantaneous deed in human words, he could not make everything come out together, suddenly, in a single utterance, in keeping with that instantaneous deed. Therefore he was compelled to say that he formed the dust and then breathed a soul into it. But if someone objects and says, “If that is so, Moses should have said that together, at the same time, God formed the dust and breathed a soul into it,” we reply to him: “If he had said that, he would have been acting as an interpreter, not as a writer.” For Moses is the writer of the book, not its interpreter. It belongs to the writer simply to write that God formed dust from the earth and breathed a soul into it. But which of them came first or afterward, and whether both were created at the same time— these inquiries and others like them are for interpreters to discuss, not for the writer. This is what we say to those who say that the body precedes the soul in its formation. We ourselves say this: neither does the soul precede the body, nor does the body precede the soul. Rather, at the very moment the seed is deposited, the soul too is immediately created out of nothing and united with it. That this is so is clear from the following demonstrations: Every beginning

is the beginning of an end, and every end belongs to a beginning. The substance of a human being is one, composed of soul and body. The substance of a human being belongs to both the beginning and the end of a human being. Thus, just as the end of a human being consists of soul and body, so the beginning necessarily consists of soul and body [?]. Therefore neither does the soul precede the body, nor does the body precede the soul. If a human being begins as seed alone, without a rational soul also being present with it, and at the end of a human being's life the body and soul are separated from one another, then human substance is not given in the same measure at a human being's beginning and end, but with addition and deficiency. There is deficiency at the beginning, but addition at the end, if a rational and incorporeal soul is not also present when the seed is deposited. And a human being is composed of soul and body, that is, of something corporeal and something incorporeal. Then this beginning is not that of a human being, but of something that is not a human being. Consequently, there is a time when a human being is not a human being. And when a soul enters it, it becomes a human being, and Socrates, or any other person whatsoever, turns out to be at one time

a human being, and at another time not a human being—a claim that is false and absurd. The book of Job, illustrious among the righteous, also bears witness that the body is formed and the soul is created within it at the same time. For he says this: “You also took clay from the earth, formed a rational living creature, and placed it on the earth.” By saying, “You formed a rational living creature,” he means that soul and body are formed without any interval. Thus these words have shown that neither does the soul precede the body, nor does the body precede the soul. Rather, together, at the same time, the body is formed from seed, and the soul is created from nothing by the Creator of all, who is God [?] and has the power to do whatever he wills. An inquiry into whether a soul is united with human seed whenever it is deposited, or not. Since we have already said that neither does the soul precede the body, nor does the body precede the soul, but both come into being together, at the same time: while the one is formed from seed, the other is created from nothing. Therefore the questioner asks this: “Whenever a man alone deposits female seed, is a soul created from nothing and united with it?” And we say no. For whenever a man alone deposits seed, or a woman alone does so, or something happens to both seeds that prevents them from producing

a conception, no soul at all is created or united with it. Rather, a soul is created and united when these three conditions are fulfilled: First, when both are deposited inside the womb; second, when they are united with one another; third, when they are bound together so that a body may be formed and composed from them. Then a soul is created. And a soul is created and united with the body. But if these three conditions are not fulfilled in the seed, no soul is created or united with them, because they are not fit to receive it. For the human body is brought to completion from both seeds. This is evident from the fact that sometimes a male is conceived, and sometimes a female, according to which of them prevails over the other. As some physicians say, when the man's seed prevails, a male is conceived, and when the woman's prevails, a female is conceived. Thus, when these three conditions are fulfilled in the seed of both, a soul is created and united with them at the Creator's command. An explanation of why the souls of infants do not distinguish good from evil and truth from falsehood. Why do the souls of infants and little children [?] not distinguish good from evil

and truth from falsehood? Is it because they are inferior in their nature or in their natural powers to the souls of youths and grown men? And we say no. Rather, these are (not) inferior in their nature to souls, nor do they lack any of the natural powers. In that, like them, they are intelligent, perceptive, capable of thought and knowledge, and so on. But because the parts of children's bodies are deficient, underdeveloped, incomplete, and unsuitable for displaying the soul's power to act through them, they fall short of displaying its power by which it distinguishes truth from falsehood or good from evil. For by its nature it can distinguish these things. But the parts of the body, which are its instruments, are deficient, incomplete, and unsuitable for displaying its power. Its discernment, by which it distinguishes good from evil or truth from falsehood, is not displayed. Thus, just as a writer does not write with a pen that has not been cut and finished, yet is not said to be unable to write, and just as a lyre player does not play a lyre that has not been properly prepared and finished, although he is skilled at playing; and just as with [?], with an adze that is not

properly prepared, finished, or suitable, a carpenter does not do carpentry, although he knows how to do carpentry and is not said to be unable to do it. So too, the soul of children does not distinguish truth from falsehood or good from evil through the incomplete parts of their bodies, because these are unsuitable. Yet by nature it has the ability to distinguish good and evil, truth and falsehood. It has this ability [?] the parts of the body move it but do not bring it into action, because they lack completeness and are unsuitable. Showing where the soul is: outside the body, inside the body, or both outside and inside the body. Some, then, make this division concerning the soul, saying that the soul is either outside the body or inside and outside. The soul is: either outside the body, inside the body, or inside and outside. They make this division, compelling the listener to answer with one of its three alternatives. Some say that it is outside the body. We say that this is not true. For if it were outside the body, it would not stir up thoughts within it.

Others say that it is inside the body. We say that this too is not true without qualification. For if it were inside the body, the body's outer parts would be empty of it. For the soul dwells throughout the whole body, and there is not a single part of it deprived of the soul or its life. “(Inside) and outside the body.” We say that this too is not true. For if it were [?] the body, it would be divisible, like air, which is inside the body and outside the body. Therefore, the soul cannot be said to be outside the body, inside the body, or both inside and outside. Rather, we say that it is throughout the whole body, united with it. Showing whether the soul is united with all the parts of the body or with one of them. Here we must investigate whether it is united and interwoven with all of them or with just one part. Medical practitioners say that it is united with the brain and dwells in it. They say that this is known from the fact that when the brain is injured, the soul's rational activities are impaired. Others say that it is united with the heart and dwells in it, and that this is known from the fact that it stirs up thoughts and reflections within it. We say that both these opinions are false. This is known from the fact that, if this were the case, a human being would be composed only of a soul and a brain, or only of a soul and a heart, and not of a soul and a body. But the claim that a human being is composed only of the brain and the soul is false. Likewise, so is the claim that a human being is composed only of the soul and the heart. Both these opinions, then, are false. We, however, say that the soul is united to the whole body: there is not a single part in it, small or large, that is deprived of the soul and its life. Rather, it is united to the whole body. That this is so is evident from the fact that a human being is composed of body and soul. An inquiry concerning the soul: when it changes from goodness to evil and from love to hatred, is it its nature that changes and is altered, or its will? Someone asks here, saying: When the soul changes from goodness to evil, and from love to

hatred, and from righteousness to injustice, and to all the other opposites of this kind, is it its nature that changes, or its will? We say that the soul’s nature does not change at all. This is evident from the following: the soul’s nature is life, as we said above, and immortality and incorporeality. Its natural powers are understanding, rationality, and the rest that we described above. It is therefore evident that the soul’s nature does not change, nor does its power of life, since it does not pass from being alive to being without life. Nor does it change from immortality to mortality, or from spiritual things to bodily things. Nor does it change from understanding to rationality. Thus the soul’s nature does not change, becoming lifeless instead of living, or bodily instead of spiritual, or mortal instead of immortal, or, instead of [?], irrational and without understanding. Rather, it is its will that changes from goodness to evil, and from obedience to disobedience, and from love to hatred, and from righteousness to injustice, and so on. An explanation

of how these three differ from one another—I mean mind, spirit, and soul. Are mind, spirit, and soul three, or two, or one? And if they are three or two, how do they differ from one another? We say that Apollinaris, who was bishop of Laodicea, said that the mind is something different from the soul. And upon this foundation [?] his doctrine; adding the other things as well, he built upon it according to his own [?]. Aristotle, however, said that the potential intellect was formed together with the human being. The actual intellect, however, enters from outside, and does not serve to make the human being’s existence complete, but is useful for advancing knowledge of the contemplation of natural things. For this reason, all human beings who have an intellect are said to be active. Plato, however, did not say that a human being consists of body and soul, but that a human being is a soul that uses a body. Others say that the mind is like the eye in the body. In the same way, the mind too is the eye of the soul, that is, its power of sight. Others have held and expressed different opinions. We, however, say that soul, spirit, and mind are one and the same, and that they are one thing,

all three of them. For these are three names that designate one particular nature and individual being. For it is clear from the following demonstrations that soul, spirit, and mind are one and the same thing. 1. If this is not so, the human being turns out to be composed of four natures: soul, I mean, mind, spirit, and body. 2. If this is not so, these three—soul, I mean, mind, and spirit—turn out to be three individual beings and three distinct natures. Which of them acts in the body, and which does not? Or do all three act? And which of the three receives recompense according to its deeds, and which does not? Do all three receive recompense? These, then, are absurdities and great follies. 3. It is clear that all three of these are one. This follows from the fact that the sacred writers said that they are one, and that they call the soul mind, and the mind soul, and the soul spirit, and the spirit soul. David, the singer of sacred songs, [?] says about the human being: “His spirit goes out, and he returns to his earth.” And his son Solomon says: “The body returns to the earth, and the spirit returns to the Lord who gave it.” And the prophet Zechariah says: “He created the human being’s spirit within him.”

Isaiah, too, says: “My soul has longed for you; even at night my spirit seeks you early.” Look, all these have named and called the soul spirit, and the spirit soul. From Saint John, bishop of Constantinople, from the commentary on the Second Letter to the Corinthians: “What, then? Is Adam dust alone? He also had another substance, akin to the beings above and incorporeal, which Scripture calls soul and spirit. Everyone knows that he also had this.” “Akin to the beings above and incorporeal, which Scripture calls soul and spirit.” “Everyone knows that he also had this.” This holy and distinguished teacher also says that Scripture calls this very same substance both soul and spirit. Saint Gregory the Theologian, too, in his discourse on the Nativity, calls the soul spirit, saying of the human being that he is “a spirit, earthly and heavenly, temporal and immortal, visible and intelligible, midway between greatness and lowliness, the very same being both spirit and flesh: spirit because of grace, flesh because of pride.” You see how he called the soul spirit. Therefore soul, spirit, and mind are one distinct nature. Demonstrating that the soul, when

it is released from the body, does not perish, but is preserved or subsists in its own existence. Thus, when the soul is released from the body to which it is bound and is separated from it, it does not perish, but is preserved or subsists independently in its own existence. That this is so is clear from the following demonstrations: 1. Everything that exists subsists either in itself or in another. Now, that which subsists in another, without possessing an existence of its own, destroys [?] that in which it subsists and constantly turns toward it, because its nature is preserved through the existence of that other thing. And if that other thing is destroyed, it too perishes. Now, while the soul is in the body, it often willingly hands the body over to tortures and death, so that it may be dissolved and destroyed. It does this to the body when it appears to the soul that this benefits it. For if it had no existence of its own when separated from the body, it would not hand the body over to perish, because it would know that when the body perished, it too would perish. But because it allows the body to die and be destroyed, we know that when it is separated from the body it possesses an existence of its own, and its own individual being subsists independently. 2. That it subsists in its own existence after separation is clear from its being a substance, as we have already demonstrated in the preceding discussions. And a substance subsists

independently, without needing another in which to subsist. 3. The body is the soul’s instrument, because through it the soul does good and evil. The one who works with an instrument is not destroyed when it casts aside its instrument. Thus, just as a carpenter is not destroyed when he puts aside his adze and saw, but is preserved and continues to exist, and just as a builder is not destroyed when he puts aside his [?], but is preserved and continues to exist, so too the soul, when it is separated from the body, which is its instrument, neither perishes nor is destroyed, but is preserved and continues to exist. Therefore, we ourselves are one thing, what belongs to us is another, and the things belonging to what is ours are another. We ourselves are the soul. What belongs to us is the body, while the things belonging to what is ours are possessions. Philosophy concerns itself with us. Medicine, however, concerns itself with what is upon us. Trades of every kind concern themselves with the things belonging to what is ours. And the things that different crafts concern themselves with have different substances. Therefore, in terms of substance, the soul is a substance distinct from the substance of the body, being separate from it and preserved on its own. 4. It is clear that the soul is preserved and continues to exist after it is separated from the body, because it is immortal, as we demonstrated in chapter sixteen. And what is not

mortal never perishes at all, but is preserved and continues to exist, both when united with another and when separated from it. 5. The Holy Scriptures testify that the soul is preserved and continues to exist after it is released from the body. God said to Moses, “I am the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.” And God is not the God of the dead, but of the living. By saying that he is not the God of the dead but of the living, he showed that their souls are alive, are preserved, and continue to exist. And Solomon said, “The dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to the Lord.” He showed that the soul is preserved, is alive, and continues to exist. And the Lord said in the Gospel, “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul.” By saying that the soul cannot be killed, he showed two things: first, that the soul is incorporeal, since it is not subject to bodily sufferings; and second, that it is immortal. What is immortal is preserved and continues to exist, neither perishing nor being destroyed. And again, he said in the account about Lazarus that, after the rich man died and was buried, the angels carried Lazarus to Abraham’s embrace, and that the rich man asked Abraham for water. Therefore, in saying, “The angels carried Lazarus to Abraham’s embrace,” [?] a word

to the rich man. Through all these things he showed that souls, when released from their bodies, are alive, are preserved, and continue to exist in their individual being. And again, Paul himself said concerning himself that he was taken up as far as the third heaven. He added, “Whether in the body or without the body, I do not know.” If his soul was taken up without his body, as he himself says, then it is clear that after the soul is separated from the body, it continues to exist and is preserved, just as the apostle’s own soul was separated from his body while remaining preserved. And again, he wrote to the Hebrews, “Remember those who are afflicted, as people who are yourselves clothed in flesh.” If, then, the one who wears is one thing, and what is worn is another, it is clear that the nature of the soul is one thing, and the nature of the body that it wears is another. And just as someone who wears a garment remains alive, is preserved, and continues to exist after taking it off, so too the soul is preserved and continues to exist after taking off the body, its garment. Showing that after the soul is separated from the body, its knowledge, perception, and memory are preserved, and that it therefore knows, perceives, and remembers after it is separated from the body. First, we must investigate who those people are who say that its knowledge is not preserved after it is separated from the body. Then we will set out

their arguments concerning this and the refutations of them. Then we will explain our own position. We say that it is the Nestorians and certain others with them who say that the soul's knowledge is not preserved after it is separated from the body. Consequently, it neither knows nor remembers. They argue for this by means of the following arguments. Their first argument is this: "If," they say, "the knowledge of souls is preserved after they are separated from bodies, then the souls of the righteous know that they have done good things and consequently rejoice, while those of the wicked know that they have done evil things and consequently are distressed. And joy and distress are bliss and torment. Then God's justice is not evident in this: souls have done good and evil things together with bodies, yet the souls enjoy bliss or suffer torment apart from their bodies, together with which they did good and evil things." But we refute this argument of theirs as follows. We say that joy and distress are not the kingdom and Gehenna, nor are they bliss and torment. For joy and distress concern the event on account of which they arise.

Take as an illustration of this those two servants of Pharaoh who were confined in prison with Joseph. Joseph said to one of them, "After three days Pharaoh will restore you to his service." But to the other he said, "After three days Pharaoh will kill you." Consequently, the one [?] began from that moment to rejoice greatly, while the other was deeply distressed. Thus the joy of the one concerning Pharaoh's service, and the distress of the other—the latter was not death itself, but distress over his death. Again, suppose a king said to two of his soldiers—to the one, "Tomorrow I will give you a hundred thousand denarii," and to the other, "I will kill you." Consequently, the one would rejoice, while the other would be distressed. We would not say that the one's joy was the hundred [?] denarii, nor that the other's distress was death itself, but rather distress over death. Likewise, the joy in which the souls of the righteous rejoice after they are separated from their bodies is not the kingdom and bliss. Nor is the distress experienced by the souls of the wicked. 1. Again, we say that joy and distress concerning an event are distinct from it, just as potentiality is distinct from actuality. As we say,

"A child is potentially a carpenter, but is not actually a carpenter." Therefore neither are joy and distress concerning any event the very event itself. Rather, they are different things. 2. Again, the bliss in the kingdom of heaven has not been seen by an eye of flesh, nor has an ear heard it, nor has it entered the human heart, as it is written. The same is true of the torment in Gehenna. But joy and distress, even though an eye of flesh has not seen them, because they are accidental qualities, have been heard by an ear of flesh and have entered the human heart. Therefore joy and distress, which accompany human souls after they are separated from the body, are not the bliss of the kingdom and the torment in Gehenna, as these people say. Their second argument is this: "The soul," they say, "has knowledge, perception, and memory by its nature when it is united with the body. Therefore, when it is released from the body, it does not have these natural attributes until it is joined with the body again, just like fire that is joined with matter. It gives heat and light, since heat and illumination belong to its nature. Therefore, when it is separated from matter, it does not give heat

or light until it is combined with matter again. So too, they say, the soul neither knows nor perceives nor remembers after it is separated from the body, until it is combined with the body again. Answer: The fire that you brought forward as an example did not, when separated from matter, lose the heat and illumination that it possessed by nature. Rather, these qualities are preserved in that fire, even though they are visible to you. Likewise, the harmony of the body is not preserved, because it is dissolved. But these qualities are preserved naturally in the soul, even though it does not display them through the body. Similarly, when an instrument is damaged in the craftsman's hand, the craftsman is not damaged along with it in what he possesses by nature. For the lyre player's speech is not cut off, nor is his voice lost, if a part of the lyre is cut off. Nor is the carpenter's finger cut off if his saw and adze are broken. Likewise, the soul does not lose what it possesses by nature because it is separated from the body. These, then, are their arguments and our answer. But first we should explain how the soul's knowledge differs from its perception, its recollection, and its memory. Once we have distinguished these four from one another, then

we will show that the soul's knowledge and memory are preserved after it is separated from the body, and that it therefore knows and remembers. The knowledge of the soul [?], then, is that by which it knows divine and human affairs, and by which it knows things that are good and evil, beneficial and harmful, and so on. To put it briefly, the soul's knowledge is the power by which it knows things. The soul's perception is not something different from its knowledge. Rather, it is its very knowledge. [?] A physical substance—that is, the body—when something cold or hot, sweet or sour, or something else of this kind touches it, perceives it when there is a soul within it, distinct from it and possessing knowledge. [?] Its perception is its very knowledge. For the soul's perceiving an event is nothing other than its knowing events. Therefore, the soul's perception is its very knowledge, and its knowledge is its very perception. Let us now show how memory differs from recollection. First, we say that events occur in three ways: some in the past, some in the present, and others

in the future. Memory, then, gathers and preserves knowledge and things learned about events that happened in the past. This is evident from the fact that no one says, 'I remember what I am seeing and hearing,' or, 'I remember what is going to happen.' Rather, one says, 'I remember what has passed.' As for events in the present, we perceive and know them through sensation and knowledge. If they are perceptible to the senses, we perceive them through the body's senses. But if they are intelligible, we know them through the soul's knowledge. Future events are objects of hope and expectation. For no one knows what is going to happen unless he has been given the gift of prophecy by God. He does not say, 'I expect and [?] that [?] will happen, or will not happen.' Memory, then, gathers and preserves things learned in the past. Recollection, however, is something preceded by forgetting. Therefore, we say that the soul has memory after it is separated from the body. Is it not recollection, then, that is attributed to the soul when it is joined to the body? For forgetfulness arises because of the body's constitution. But memory

belongs to the soul when it is joined to the body, when it is being released from it, and after it has been released from it. We should also show what led some people to say that the soul's memory ceases after it is released from the body. And we say: Was it not because its recollection ceases? And because they supposed that memory was recollection, they said that memory ceases. But we say that these differ greatly from one another, since forgetfulness is an affection of the body. And recollection follows forgetfulness. Therefore recollection too is an affection of the body. Memory, however, is a natural affection of the soul. For this reason it does not cease in the soul when the soul is released from the body. Now that these things have been distinguished and clearly demonstrated, now, as for its knowledge and memory being preserved after it separates from the body, and its therefore knowing and remembering: that this is so is evident from the following demonstrations. First, some of the soul's powers are natural, while others are nonessential. The natural ones are understanding, thought, knowledge, reason, [?], memory, and the rest. The nonessential ones are anger, desire, perception through the five senses, imagination, and things like these, as we demonstrated in the tenth chapter. When, therefore, the soul separates from the body, the nonessential powers

undoubtedly cease in it, because they occurred in it on account of the body. But the natural powers do not cease in it at all after it is released from the body. This is evident for two reasons. One is that they are naturally implanted in it. The other is that if these natural powers cease in it, its nature ceases. For its nature, which is life, consists of nothing other than these powers. Are these powers themselves anything other than its nature? For it is not a body, such that its natural powers would be something apart from its nature. Rather, it is spiritual and without a body. Therefore its nature is to live, understand, think, know, reason, move itself, and remember. Therefore the soul's knowledge and memory are preserved after it separates from the body. Secondly, we say: the wise [?] that reason has two forms. One gathers knowledge, while the other retains what has been gathered. They called the gathering faculty thought, and they named the retaining faculty memory. Reason is a power of the soul, both while it dwells in the body and when it departs from it. It possesses this power. And reason has these two powers— I mean the gathering and the retaining faculties. Therefore, when the soul separates from the body, it thinks and remembers what it did

here. Thirdly, there is reduction to absurdity: if the soul has no knowledge or memory after it separates from [?], we ought not to commemorate the departed, as the canons of the apostles command us. Paul commanded as follows in his canon: that the commemoration of those who have fallen asleep should be celebrated on the third day, because on the third day our Lord rose from the tomb; and on the ninth day, in remembrance of those who are living and those who have died. And for thirty days, according to the old law. For Moses, then, the Hebrews [?] for thirty days.
