If the soul has no knowledge or memory after it is separated from the body, then the deacon needlessly and uselessly proclaims at the offering, during the holy mysteries, “Let us remember those who have already fallen asleep.” But the soul’s knowledge and memories are preserved after it is released from the body. It would not be right for us, who are Christians, to ask the souls of the martyrs and saints to plead with God on our behalf, if the soul’s memory were not preserved, and its knowledge after it is released from the body. The souls of the holy believers and the souls of the wicked and the good are brought to one place and one chamber until the day of resurrection. For if [?], and they neither know nor distinguish, it is all the same to them

whether they remain and are kept in one place or in many places, in bright places or in dark places. But if the souls of the saints and of the wicked are brought to separate places—the former to bright chambers and into the company of angels, and the latter to dark chambers and into the company of demons—it is evident that the soul’s knowledge and memory are preserved. Therefore, to eliminate these absurdities, it is clear and readily apparent that souls have knowledge and memory after they are released from their bodies. And consequently they know and remember. And fourth: this is known from the testimony of the Holy Scriptures. For our Lord says this in the Gospel, in the account of the rich man and Lazarus: “Lazarus died, and the angels carried him to Abraham’s embrace. The rich man also died and was buried. While he was being tormented in Sheol, he lifted his eyes and saw Abraham far away, and Lazarus in his embrace. He raised his voice and said, ‘My father Abraham, have mercy on me! Send Lazarus to dip his finger in water and moisten my tongue, because I am being tormented in this flame.’ He said to him, ‘My son, remember that you received your good things during your lifetime, and Lazarus his bad things. Besides all this, a great chasm stands between us, and those

who wish to cross from your side to ours cannot, nor can they cross from our side to yours.’ He said to him, ‘I ask you to send him to my father’s house, for I have five brothers. Let him go and warn them, so that they too do not come to this place of torment.’” And so on. By saying that the angels carried Lazarus to Abraham’s embrace, he showed two things. First, that the soul continues in its own individual existence after it is released from the body; and second, that angels carry the souls of the saints. The rich man’s lifting his eyes is an act of the soul’s will; therefore its will is preserved. His seeing Abraham is an act of knowledge. His crying out and saying, “My father Abraham, have mercy on me,” is clearly an act of the soul; therefore its rational faculty is preserved. For the apostle Paul says, “For me, life is Christ, and if I die, it is gain for me.” That is, the apostle compares his life here with his life after death and says: If his soul knew, understood, and remembered while it dwelt in his body, but after it was released from the body, or when he died, his soul neither knew nor understood nor remembered, this would be a loss and a detriment to it. How,

then, could “if I die, it is gain for me” be true? And if, just as his soul knew, understood, and remembered while it dwelt in the body, Thus, after it was separated from the body, how could he say, “It is gain for me if I die”? This is loss, not gain. But it is known and clear that after the soul is released from its body and the body dies, it knows and understands more, and thinks and remembers more. From his statement, “If I die, it is gain for me.” Therefore, when the soul is released from the body, it knows, understands, and remembers more than when it was in the body. An inquiry into whether, just as the body sees with the eyes, hears with the ears, and acts differently with its other parts, so too the soul sees with one part, but hears and knows with another, or whether this is otherwise for it. Someone asks and investigates, saying, “Just as the body sees with the eyes, hears with the ears, and smells with the nostrils, and acts differently with its other parts, is it the same with the soul? Does it see with one part, but hear with another, and know and understand with another? Or is this otherwise for it?” First, then, we investigate why the body sees only with the eyes and does not see with its whole self, and why

it hears only with the ears, and why it smells only with the nostrils and not with its whole self. Afterward we speak about the soul: how the whole of it hears, sees, understands, and knows. The body, then, sees only with the eyes because they have an affinity with the light of the sun, since their composition differs from that of the whole body. In what way? The eye is pure, clear, bright, shining, and radiant. Through these qualities it has an affinity with the light of the sun, since the light of the sun is pure, clear, bright, shining, and radiant. Therefore, when the sunlight remains upon the eye, it enables it to see because of the affinity it has with it. Likewise, those who dig [?] in the ground, when they are deprived of sunlight and darkness reigns over them, bring a highly polished bronze basin and place it beneath [?] the opening of these [?]. Then the basin receives the sunlight from above because of the affinity the bronze has with the light, since it is smooth, pure, and very radiant; and the basin reflects that light. Thus it sends it to this side and that side until it gives light to those digging the ground. Also upon

pure, shining silver, and also upon water that is pure, clear, and shining, when the sunlight falls upon them, they transmit a certain bright ray that falls upon a nearby wall. Therefore it is clear that this is why, out of the whole body, the eye alone sees: because it has an affinity with the light of the sun. The ears, however, hear alone, while the whole body does not hear, for this reason: their openings are pierced through from the outside as far as the brain, and there is nothing in between. When the air is set in motion, it makes the sound fine and is not stopped until it brings it into the openings of the ears and strikes the brain with it, and it is perceived. Likewise, for another reason, the nose alone smells, and not the whole body as well. Therefore, because the body is composed of different or numerous parts, it does not see with its whole self, nor does it hear or smell with its whole self. Rather, it sees with one part, hears with another, smells with another, and with another acts differently and feels by touch. But the soul is not like this. Rather, the whole of it sees, the whole of it hears, and the whole of it understands and knows. That this is so is clear from the fact that it is

simple and spiritual. And what is simple and spiritual is not composed of parts. And so it does not have parts with which it sees, others with which it hears, and others with which it knows. It understands as a whole and knows as a whole. The angels are also like this: each one of them sees as a whole, hears as a whole, and knows as a whole. So when the soul is separated from the body, it sees as a whole and hears as a whole. It knows and understands as a whole, and it senses and remembers as a whole, because it is spiritual, bodiless, simple, and not composite. On what the soul knows and what it does not know when it is separated from the body. When the soul is separated from the body, it understands and knows these things: It knows itself, and it knows that it is created. It knows that it has a Creator, and it knows that it was in the body. It knows that it has departed from it, and it knows that it will receive its own body on the day of resurrection. It recognizes the angels and demons when they assemble at its departure from the body. It recognizes the souls who are in the place where it stays with them until the resurrection. It knows what it did here, whether good or evil, and it knows what is reserved for it,

whether delight or torment. It also knows and is aware of the offerings made on its behalf. The soul knows these things and things like them after it is released from the body. That this is so is known from the fact that its knowledge, perception, understanding, memory, and the rest of its natural faculties are preserved after it departs from the body. But the soul does not know these other things after it is released from the body: It does not know what we do here after it departs, and it does not know whether times are good or bad for us. Nor does it know the punishments sent upon us by God, or things far away from it. The soul does not know these things after it departs from the body, nor does it know similar things. That this is so is known from the fact that the soul is limited, and therefore its knowledge is necessarily limited too. For one whose nature is unlimited also has unlimited knowledge, while one whose nature is limited also has limited knowledge. Thus God's nature is unlimited, and so is his knowledge. But angels and souls have limited natures, and their knowledge is limited too. And if the soul's knowledge is limited, just as its nature is limited,

then after it departs from the body, it does not know what we do here, or the circumstances we are in, or things far away from it, unless this knowledge is given to it as a gift from God, just as he gave prophecy to the prophets, and they foresaw future and distant things with the eyes of prophecy and spoke about them. So if this knowledge is given to the soul as a gift from God, who is almighty, it knows. But it truly knows, in its own right, those other things we mentioned above, because its natural faculties, by which it knows them, are preserved. On those who assemble and gather around the soul when it is released from the body. We say that angels and demons gather and assemble around it and meet it. Why, then, do they assemble around it and meet it? We say that the angels gather around it because they want it to go with them, and therefore they recount its good deeds. Likewise, the demons also gather around it because they want it to go with them, and therefore they recount its evil deeds. And it is known that angels and demons gather and assemble around the soul when it is separated from the body

and meet it, from these trustworthy testimonies: In the Gospel, the Lord speaks as follows to those who did not feed him or care for him through the poor: “Go away from me, you who are cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.” He also said in the account of the rich man and Lazarus that when Lazarus died, the angels carried him to Abraham’s bosom. Jude the apostle also spoke in his general epistle about the dispute that Satan, the adversary, had with the angel Michael over the burial of Moses, saying: “Michael, the archangel, when he was speaking with the devil and disputing about the body of Moses, did not dare to bring an abusive accusation against him, but said to him, ‘May the Lord rebuke you.’” This is also known from the account of Anthony the hermit, which Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, and Saint Severus of Antioch relate as follows: Once, when Anthony was about to eat bread, he stood up to pray at the ninth hour and sensed

that his mind had been lifted up. He thought that he was outside his body, and he saw himself being raised into the air. He was being taken toward God, while peaceful angels who loved humanity went ahead of him and accompanied him. When he had traveled part of the journey, he saw others, gloomy and bitter, who glared fiercely and terribly. They came and stood against him in the air, setting up checkpoints for him [?] and preventing him from passing. They said to him, “We are detaining you because you owe us for these things.” When those demons wanted to recount his deeds from his birth onward, the angels accompanying him rebuked them and said: “The Lord, through his grace, has wiped away all his shortcomings and sins from his birth until he became a monk. But as for his conduct and his victories since he became a monk and pledged himself to God, you are now too weak to attack, and you have no grounds for any accusation.” Then they all fled and scattered, and like smoke

they vanished. His way was cleared and became unobstructed. Thus his soul was raised until it reached the place it reached. After this, his thoughts gathered within him again, and it seemed to him that he had returned to his body and was wholly in his cell. Amazed in his mind, he thanked God for what had happened. He marveled greatly at how the evil powers fight against us and against the soul after it separates from the body, and at the bitter hatred they have toward it. Because of this, he forgot his food, although his stomach was faint with hunger. A longing drew him to find out for certain whether what he had seen was true or not. For this reason he subjected his body to severe ascetic discipline. The old man made his body toil through virtuous practices. Therefore, one night Christ called to him, saying, “Anthony, come, go outside and see.” When he went outside, he saw something like a man standing in the middle of the earth, whose height reached up to heaven. In appearance

he was terrifying and hideous, and his ugliness exceeded even his size. Around him he saw a great multitude flying up from the earth and rising on wings. Those in front flew as far as his hands, and then fell and were thrust downward. Some, however, flew and rose above his arms and escaped his grasp. He rejoiced greatly and took pleasure in those who flew and fell beneath him, but he was greatly distressed and embittered over those who rose above him. He was gnashing his teeth and growing furious. When Anthony saw this vision, Christ immediately said to him: “Understand what is being shown to you.” Immediately he understood that what was being shown to him in the vision was the passage of souls. For that tall man was the devil, the ruler of the air and of the spirit, as the apostle Paul said of him. Those who were flying and falling beneath him were those who, in the snares of sin,

had become entangled, had been stained by various kinds of wickedness, and had been caught in his trap. But those who were flying and rising above him were those who had cast off the passions of the flesh and the earthly weight of sin, and had escaped his snares. Through holy conduct they flew to heaven. It is therefore clear from these things that when the soul separates from the body, angels and demons gather and assemble around it. Athanasius of Alexandria further relates concerning Saint Anthony that his eagerness to excel and practice asceticism increased in his old age. Thus, once while he was on the mountain, he raised his eyes to heaven and suddenly saw someone ascending. Fear and amazement fell upon him. He called blessed the one who had been found worthy of this ascent, and asked the Lord to make known to him who it was. He heard a voice from heaven saying, “This is the soul of Ammon, who lived in the region of Nitria.” This man was holy and excellent, an outstanding monk from his youth to his old age, whose end became greater

than his beginning. From the region of Nitria, where he lived, to the mountain where Anthony lived was a journey of thirteen days, as they say. The holy teachers also testify that when the soul separates from the body, angels and demons assemble around it and encounter it. From Saint Dionysius, one of the judges of the Areopagus, bishop of the city of Athens, from the letter to Demophilus, a member of the covenant: We ought to know that [?] they attempt to enter a person. Have they not already approached him in this way? And, conversely, to benefit a person, as they wished. For they have filled their own souls, in every case, with either divine virtue or brutish passions. These virtuous people become associates and companions of the angels here and there, and inherit with them a blessed dwelling in that incorruptible world. They are with God forever and ever, which is greater and higher than all good things. But those others fall completely away from that divine peace which was theirs. Both here and after their death, they are gathered together with brutish demons. For this reason, then, we ought to take great care to be with our Lord at all times, and not with demons.

From Saint Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, from the Homily of Admonition: I do not forget, my brothers, what fear, trembling, and distress we must experience when the soul separates from the body. For the opposing powers gather against it: the rulers of darkness who hold sway over the world of wickedness, authorities and dominions, and spirits of wickedness. Then they seize the soul amid terror, bringing before it all the sins it committed, knowingly and unknowingly, from its youth until the time when it was seized. They stand and bring accusations concerning everything it has done. And again, the powers of God come and stand face to face with the opposing powers, and they too recount the soul’s good deeds. And now, how much trembling do you think it experiences at that hour, until the verdict comes and it is set free? From Saint Severus, from the letter to Thomas, bishop of Beth Garmai: For when the soul is separated from the body, after its departure from the body, the good angelic powers and the company of evil demons encounter it, so that, according to the effect of the good deeds, those which it performed, whether good or evil,

either these or those will receive it into the appropriate places, to be kept until the last day, on which we all rise, either to judgment or to everlasting life, and are led either to the flame of unquenchable fire or to the kingdom of heaven, which has no end. From the book of Isaiah, who wrote about the joy experienced by the soul that wishes to submit to God: For when the soul leaves this world, angels go with it. Then the powers of darkness come out to meet it, wishing to seize it and examine it. If they have anything of their own in it, then it is not the angels who fight against them; rather, the deeds it performed shelter it and protect it from them, so that they cannot approach it. But if its deeds are pure, then the angels [?] before it until it meets God with joy. Then, at that hour, it forgets the deeds of this world and all its toil. From Saint Mar Jacob, bishop of Edessa, from the discourse on the formation of the human being: After the discussion of graves and human life in this world, then, what death is, and decay in the grave, and the dissolution and disintegration of the body’s members within the earth, and the scattering of our bones toward

Sheol. He said: While the body is dissolved into dust according to God’s decree, each of the elements then departs to join its own kind: water, air, and fire, until truly only dust remains, alongside the earth and dust of its own kind. But the soul departs either to the souls of the righteous or to the souls of the wicked, together with the dark [?] of the rebellious demons, immediately, according to the decree issued concerning it by God, until the time arrives for the resurrection of the whole human race, and for judgment and the just recompense owed to everyone according to their deeds and according to their conduct or actions here. Look, the distinguished teachers of the orthodox faith have clearly shown us that when the soul is separated from the body, angels and demons assemble and gather around it. They encounter it, and the angels bring forward its good deeds because they want it to go with them, while the demons accuse it of its evil deeds because they want it to go with them. A refutation of those who say that souls wander and pass from body to body, showing that their belief is false. Some of

the pagans say that souls wander and pass from body to body according to the good and evil things they have done. They say that if a soul has done good things, it passes from the body in which it did those good things into another body, better and more beautiful than the first. But if it has done evil things, it passes from that body into another body, inferior and uglier than the one in which it did those evil things. But we say that what they claim is false and contemptible. This is evident from the following: (1) The soul possesses knowledge and memory. For knowledge and memory are natural powers of the soul, as we showed in the preceding discussions. Therefore it knows what it has done and also remembers it. And if it moved and passed from body to body, when it passed into one of these bodies, it would remember there what it had done in the body from which it had departed. Yet we know that the souls united with human bodies today do not remember being in other bodies, or doing either good or evil in them. But if they object and say that knowledge and memory belong neither to the soul alone nor to the body alone, but to both together,

we have answered this objection in chapter thirty-three, which shows that the soul's knowledge and memory are preserved after it separates from the body. (2) For souls that pass from body to body, one of two things necessarily follows: either God transfers them, or they transfer themselves. If God transfers them as recompense for good and evil, he does not act justly. For the soul's powers depend on the body's constitution. Consequently, it does good and evil through the body. It would therefore be right for him to transfer, along with the souls, the bodily constitutions with which they did good and evil. But if the souls themselves pass from body to body, they do so either by nature or by choice. If they pass by nature, twenty of them would have to pass into a single place suited to them. But if they do so by choice, they would have to pass into bodies subject to suffering and chosen by them, if their passage lay within their own choice. These, then, are among the arguments from nature showing that souls do not pass from body to body. The testimonies from the Holy Scriptures are these: David, the prophet and singer of sacred songs, says, “My soul thirsts for you, the living God. When shall I come and see your face?”

His son Solomon says, “The body returns to the earth, and the spirit to the Lord who gave it.” Our Lord says of Lazarus in the Gospel that he died and the angels carried him to Abraham's bosom. Stephen, the foremost and first of the martyrs, said as he was being stoned, “Our Lord Jesus Christ, receive my spirit.” And Paul the apostle said, “I long to depart, so that I may be with Christ.” Thus, through all these things, it has been established that souls do not pass from body to body or move from one bodily form to another. Showing where souls remain until the day of resurrection
Someone asks, “When human souls depart from their bodies, where do they remain until the resurrection?” Some say that they are in this air between us and heaven, and that they remain there until the day of resurrection. But Saint John of Constantinople rejects this opinion, and we agree with him and say that it is not true. That it is not true is evident from the following proofs. (1) If souls are in this air after separating from their bodies, why do we say that there is another world? We would not

then need another world if they are in this air. (2) That they are not in this air is evident from the fact that the angels carried poor Lazarus to Abraham's bosom, as our Lord said. And from the fact that the rich man asked that he come and testify to his brothers, but this was not permitted. And from the fact that, when that other rich man wanted to tear down his storehouses, he was told, “This very night they will take your soul from you.” And from what David said to God: “When shall I come and see your face?” And also from what the apostle Paul said: “I long to depart and be with Christ.” Therefore, when souls depart from bodies, they do not remain in this air until the day of resurrection, as these people have said. Others, however, say that the souls of the upright, the righteous, the apostles, the martyrs, the saints, and others like them, when they depart from bodies, mingle with the angels and remain with them until the day of resurrection. But the souls of the wicked and the unjust remain with demons and mingle with them—with them—until the day of resurrection. We, however, say that this is true in fact and time;

we acknowledge it and also believe it. But this is not enough to resolve the question and the perplexity. For the question demands this: where, in what place, do souls remain when they are separated from bodies, before the day of resurrection? Others, however, say that when souls are separated from bodies, they are not in a place, because they are spiritual and without bodies. And what is spiritual and without a body does not need a place in which to exist. Therefore, they say, when souls are separated from bodies, they are not in a place. First, however, we should speak about space and place. After that we shall discuss whether or not souls are in places when they are separated from bodies. Let us therefore say what space is. We say that philosophers have held many opinions about space. Some of them say that it is length and breadth alone. Therefore, [?] perceived by the senses, but it is known by the mind. Some of them said that space is what encloses the boundaries of a body. Others said that space is what lies between

the earthenware vessel and the wine, and what lies between a body and the air: something conceived as existing between the earthenware vessel and the wine, and between the water and the pot, and between a person's body and the surrounding air. Others thought differently and said about space that it is not a place. [?] to gather together their views and opinions about space. These, then, concern the question of what space is. A place, however, is space conjoined with a substance, such as the place in which someone sits or lies down. For we say that John necessarily stands in a place, and that Socrates wrote in a place, in any event. These remarks about space and place are sufficient for the present. Let us now examine whether souls, when they depart from bodies, need space and a place in which to exist or not. We say that bodies need space and [?] in which to exist, because they are composite and require length, height, and breadth, and they also have boundaries. But what is incorporeal, because it is not [?] and has neither length nor [?] nor breadth, needs neither space nor place.

But if this is so, someone may perhaps say, “Then those mentioned above who said that souls are not in a place when they are separated from bodies are right.” We say that “place” is spoken of in two senses: a place suitable for bodies to exist in. And there is a place suitable for an incorporeal being to exist in, because everything finite necessarily needs a place. Therefore angels are finite. And because they are finite, they necessarily exist in a place. Now place, as it applies to bodies, is spoken of in ten ways: above, below, to the right, to the left, in front, behind, here, there, nearby, and far away. Every body that exists, then, is in one of these places. But the place of souls is none of these. Rather, the place of souls is spiritual [?] and subtle, suitable for souls to exist in. Thus souls that have separated and departed from bodies also exist in a place, necessarily. So the question still remains: Where, in what place, does a soul exist until the resurrection? And we say that the souls of the righteous, the just, and the holy are in paradise, from which

Adam departed. But the souls of the apostles, the martyrs, and the [?], those who are closer to God, are above heaven. But the souls of the wicked and the unjust are in dark places beneath the earth until the resurrection. Others, however, say that the souls of the wicked are in regions of darkness until the resurrection, but those of the just, the righteous, the apostles, the martyrs, and the true believers who lived virtuous lives are in paradise until the resurrection, from the time they depart from their bodies. This is clear from the fact that God brought the robber’s soul there when he said to him, “Today you will be with me in paradise.” This is also clear from the testimonies [?] of the orthodox teachers concerning this. From Saint Gregory the Theologian, from the discourse on Easter: “At the time of his saving work in the Passion, the divinity did not withdraw from either part, for God’s gifts are [?], even though it separated the soul from the body by its own will. And it remained in both. For it revealed the body by its not undergoing the decay that comes from death. It released it, and what the dominion of death had held

in its power. Through the soul, however, it prepared a way for the robber to the region of paradise. Both things are accomplished together through both, while the good divinity also acted [?]. Through the body’s incorruptibility it released the body; and through the soul, which made use of its own dwelling place, it brought about humanity’s return to paradise.” And from Saint John, bishop of Constantinople, from the discourse on the tree from which Adam ate being called the knowledge of good and evil: “The robber entered paradise, we say. And what does this amount to? Are these, then, the [?] that God promised us? Do you not hear the divine Paul saying, ‘Those good things that no eye has seen and no ear has heard, and that have not entered the human heart’? But paradise is something the eye has seen, the ear has heard of, and the human heart has conceived. For we have been speaking about such things for many days now. How, then, was the robber rewarded in this way? For God promised [?] to bring us not into paradise, but into heaven itself. Nor did they proclaim the kingdom of paradise, but the kingdom of heaven. For he began

to proclaim and say, ‘Repent; the kingdom has drawn near’—rather, ‘the kingdom of heaven.’ If, then, he promised the kingdom of heaven, but brought the robber into paradise, he has not yet given him his reward.” From Saint Philoxenus of Mabbug: “For when our Lord was hanging on the cross for us, and two robbers were crucified with him, it is written that the robber on the right believed in him and said to him, ‘Remember me, Lord, when you come in your kingdom.’ And immediately Jesus promised him and said to him, ‘Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in paradise.’ And a little later: He immediately took the soul of [?] and, as he had promised him, brought it with him into Paradise. The souls of all the righteous were around him. And he taught that it would enjoy bodily refreshment in the tomb. And he went in to the bodies that were in the tombs. And they gave them the good news that they would rise. [?] And through his soul he visited the souls of the righteous and of sinners, some of them in Paradise, and some of them in Sheol. And he promised them a return to their bodies. And after other things: For when

he went to Paradise and took the robber’s soul to be with him—the one who remained on the cross—he removed the cherub and the blade of the sword that had been guarding Paradise. He brought in with him the souls of all the righteous who had been wandering outside, because the guards had not allowed them to enter. And there, through his soul, [?] they proclaimed salvation and a return to their bodies. [?] He removed the cherub alone, but also gathered them and brought them into Paradise. And through his word he assured them of the resurrection of their bodies. From then until now, and onward until the world ends, every soul of one of the righteous that departs from the body enters Paradise and lives there until the time of his coming. But the souls of sinners are in Sheol. For this reason Scripture also says that he went there. When God went to Paradise through his soul, not only the souls of the righteous [?], but also, as I believe, the angels themselves. For even of the one who is great among the angels, it is not written that he entered it, but only that he guarded it from outside. How, then, can we not confidently say that none of these other spiritual powers were allowed to enter there either? Showing

with which ranks and orders souls mingle when they are separated from their bodies. With which orders and ranks do human souls mingle before the resurrection, when they are released from their bodies and depart from them? We say that the souls of the righteous, the apostles, and the martyrs, or of the prophets, the just, and the saints, are with the angels when they depart from their bodies, and mingle with them until the resurrection. For the angels dwell above heaven and also in Paradise. But the souls of the wicked and the unjust, when they are separated from their bodies, are with the demons and mingle with them until the resurrection. We know that this is so from the following indications. The first is evident from the principle of justice. For those souls which, while they are in bodies in this world, practice virtuous ways of life that resemble those of the angels and please them, mingle with the angels when they are released from their bodies, and are with them as with those to whom they rightly belong and whom they have loved. But those souls which, while they dwell [?] upon them and have loved. But those souls which, while they were dwelling in the body in this world, practiced ways of life

that were evil and shameful, pleasing the demons and making them glad, rightly mingle with the demons when they are released from their bodies, and are with them as with those to whom they rightly belong and whom they have loved. A second indication is also evident from the fact that, when the soul is released and leaves the body, angels assemble and come to it, as do demons. They gather on two opposing sides, and each of them wants that soul to go with him. They fight over this, as we have shown in chapter thirty-six. Saint Athanasius, bishop of the city of Athens, from the letter to Demophilus, a member of the covenant: One should recognize those who try to walk among people [?]. Not from this [?]. Look, already [?] they hoped in him, and in opposition to this, to do good to someone [?]. For whatever they desired, they certainly caused to dwell within themselves [?]. And he concludes in chapter thirty-six, and so on. An inquiry into which was created in the image of God—the soul, the body, or both together—and what the image and likeness of God are in which the human being was created. Which is in the image of God:

the soul, the body, or both together? We say that it is the soul alone. This is known from God. 1. God is [?], without a body, incorruptible, and immortal. Which, then, of these two is his image: the soul, which is simple, incorporeal, immortal, and incorruptible, or the body, which is composite, bodily, corruptible, and mortal? It is clear that it is the soul, not the body. 2. Which is in the image of God: the body, which has male and female forms, or the soul, which is above these things? It is clear that it is the soul. 3. If the body, which is composed of elements, were the image of God, irrational animals would also be in the image of God. This is an impious and false claim. Thus, through these arguments, it has become clear that the soul alone is in the image of God. We must now inquire in what respect the soul is in the image of God. We say that the soul is in the image of God in these respects, and we say that it is in these ways: 1. God is not a body, is not bodily, is invisible and immortal. So too is the soul. 2. Just as God sees everything as its Lord and in reality,

so too the soul sees everything in imagination, but not in reality. Another point: Just as God rules over created things—and it says, “Rule over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the sky,” and so forth—the freedom and self-government that he gave to the soul. For just as God does whatever he wishes among the things possible for him. 4. In that bodily creatures serve the human being, and [?] creatures praise God their Creator, whether bodily or incorporeal. 5. The fact that the human being practices crafts, builds houses, and creates like God. This is possible for angels, but not for animals, which lack reason. 6. The fact that he granted the human being to stand in his place in this universe, like a servant who stands in his master's place in his city and in his house. 7. God performs mighty works and wonders: I mean that he raises the dead and cleanses lepers, gives sight to the blind, closes and opens the heavens, and so forth. God does these things by nature, but in his grace he has also granted this to the human being as a gift. Just as God is present in his creation, acts upon it, and governs it without being seen, so too the soul is present in the body [?] and acts

within it and governs it [?], without being seen. 8. God said, “Let us make the human being in our image,” that is, in the form in which God the Word was to become flesh and become a complete human being without change. As the divine apostle says, “The first man is dust, from the earth; the second man is the Lord from heaven.” And therefore, just as the human being is composed of soul and body, one person and one composite nature, so too Christ, from divinity and humanity, is one person and one composite nature. As the very same apostle Paul said, “Just as the children shared in flesh and blood, so too God the Word shared in humanity.” That is, he said this: just as the soul of children together with flesh and blood is one person and one composite nature, so too God the Word together with living flesh [?] is one person and one composite nature. 9. God is three persons. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The Father is unbegotten, the Son is begotten, and the Spirit proceeds. In this image, therefore,

he also created the three persons in humanity—I mean Adam, Eve, and Seth. He created Adam unbegotten, and Seth begotten, and Eve proceeding. These are some of the ways concerning the images of God in which humanity was created. Now let us examine further in what way humanity is the likeness of God, because it is written that God said, “Let us make humanity in our image and likeness.” We say that God is good, just, holy, and merciful by nature. He therefore made humanity to resemble him in his goodness, justice, holiness, and mercy, as far as it is possible to resemble him. Thus a human being should be good, just, holy, and merciful, as our Lord said in the Gospel: “Be merciful, as your Father in heaven is merciful.” But let us examine further how the body is called the image of God. It is called this because of its union with the soul. Because of its union, therefore, the soul [?] its own properties to the body, and receives and takes on those of the body. Because of this union, the whole human being is said to be in the image and likeness of God.

For the name “human being” denotes the composite of soul and body. Thus blessed Moses also wrote as follows: God said to him, “Let us make human beings in our image and likeness.” As long as the soul is bound to the body and united with it, it grants the body the designation “image and likeness of God” because of their union. But when it is released from the body, it no longer grants it this. Thus the soul, in and of itself, is properly the image and likeness of God. The body, however, is called the image and likeness of God because of its union and participation, and in a borrowed sense. Chapter showing that the departed benefit from the offerings made on their behalf. From the history of solitaries written by Palladius, bishop of Helenopolis. A certain man withdrew from this world. He had a wife and also a daughter, who died while she was still among the hearers. Her father distributed the share that fell to her as alms to the poor. Her mother, for her part, also never ceased pleading with God for her daughter, who had departed from the world unbaptized. While he was praying, a voice was heard saying to him, “Your daughter has been baptized. Do not grieve.” But he did not believe. So that unseen voice spoke again:

“Dig up her grave.” He dug it up and did not find her, for she had been moved and laid among the faithful. Saint John of Constantinople, from the forty-first homily on the First Letter to the Corinthians: “But if they departed as sinners, you should rejoice for this reason: they have been cut off from sins and have not added to their evil deeds. And you should help them as far as you can, not with tears, but with prayers and supplications, and with alms and offerings. For this practice did not arise without reason, nor is it in vain that we commemorate those who have departed before the divine mysteries and make offerings on their behalf, petitioning this Lamb who lies before us, who took away the sin of the world. Rather, we do this so that consolation may come to them through it. Nor is it in vain that the one standing at the altar, when the mighty mysteries are being celebrated, cries out, ‘On behalf of all those who have fallen asleep in Christ, and on behalf of those whose commemorations are being celebrated.’ For if commemorations were not held on their behalf, For these practices of ours are not a theatrical performance—far from it! These things are carried out at the command of the Spirit. Let us therefore help them and perform commemorations on their behalf. For if the sacrifices their father offered purified Job’s children, why do you dispute that, when we too make offerings on behalf of those who have died, they receive some consolation? For it is customary for

God to grant gifts to some for the sake of others. Paul shows this when he says, “So that, from many persons, the gift bestowed on us may be acknowledged with thanksgiving [?] by many on their behalf.” Therefore, do not grow weary of us when we help those who have died, make offerings on their behalf, and ask that prayers be offered for them. Then we also name them along with the martyrs, along with the confessors, along with the priests. For we are all one body, even though some members are more glorious than others. And it is possible to gather forgiveness for them from every quarter: from prayers, from the offerings made on their behalf, and from those along with whom they are named. Why, then, are you distressed? Why are you mourning, when you can gather all this forgiveness for the person who has died? By the same author. By the same author, from the sixty-second homily of the Commentary on the Gospel of John. For if the person who died was a sinner and greatly angered God, it is right to weep—that is, not merely to weep, for this does not help him at all, but to do things that can bring him consolation: almsgiving and offerings. Honor the dead person, not with lamentations and wailing,

but with praises and songs, and by conducting yourself properly [?]. For the person who has departed is accompanied by angels, even if someone [?]. But if someone is impure, even if the whole city accompanies him, he will not be exalted. I want you to honor the person who has departed. Honor him in another way: by giving alms. By the same author, from the third homily of the Commentary on the Epistle to the Philippians: It was not without purpose that the apostle established as a rule that those who have died should be commemorated at the awe-inspiring mysteries. For we know that they receive many benefits, and no small advantage. For when all the people stand with their hands outstretched, together with the priestly assembly, and the awe-inspiring divine sacrifice lies before us, how shall we not persuade God when we plead on their behalf? That we can give to the poor on their behalf. For this action brings consolation. God made us because he wanted us to benefit from one another. For why did he command us to pray for peace

But if you examine this, discerning scholar, and find unusual words or errors, or take offense at them, correct them as far as your understanding allows. But do not let your heart become angry with me, giving room for blame and disregarding the apostolic saying, and do not become vexed because of my lack of learning, for I was caught up in the distraction of ignorance and the circle of difficulty. Instead, remember love, which is the bond of perfection, and remember me, a sinner, with a word that will benefit me, so that I may receive mercy from [?], the one who finds the lost. And as you remember me with kindness, may you too be forgiven and have your reward multiplied many times over, as you utter a word of forgiveness for me from your mouth, and also for those who have cared for me. And by remembering my fathers in body and in spirit, you fulfill the apostle’s saying—that is, his command—that we should pray earnestly for one another so that we may be healed.

These were written on Sunday, the eighth day of October, in the year one thousand five hundred and forty-six, in the northern monastery of Mar Barsauma, near the villages of Hashri and Bagdashi, in the God-fortified region of [?].
